#485 1 2004-07-11T16:06:04Z brickman
If you look up at the top of this forum, you will see a two page thread about weapons. I have also seen a thread somewhere about network play. So I had an idea: competitive swordplay 2 player. I know, I'm not the first to think of this, but I'm gonna back it up with an idea of how it works.
First, each player has a "health" bar, which takes the place of the time bar but goes dwon with hits instead of time. Each starts with 10 full points (ten secs). Gold randomly appears somewhere every 15 seconds and heals whoever gets it 2 points.
Each player has two attack buttons added to the movement ones (fortunately, the n movement system is simple enough that this won't cause problems if two ppl use one keyboard). The first button is stab, second slash. On the groundd, stab does 1 damage fast, slash does 2 but is slower. In the air, slash does 1.5 in front of you and stab does 3 BELOW YOU, but only if you hit it while going down. Thus, in order to win you have to always stay above your opponenet and off the ground, encouraging people to still use n's physics instead of just swordplay.
In order to take full advantage of n's physics, you couldn't just do dm. Mabey additional modes like one where one player starts with a 3 second health bar and no sword and the other is hooked up to a 20 second timer (chase), or where each player's sword starts in the middle of the map and they must get to it fast to gain an advantage over their opponent (race).
People would be able to make their own maps for this, and specify the modes it works for. It would allso come with one or two maps per mode. The players would obviously be different colors (or mabey just a floating number above their head).

What do you think? It may be a lot of work, but its the only multiplayer mode that would do justice to the n engine.

Enemies. First, make the AI refresh rate constant so I don't stumble upon a cool situation in ned and then loose it when making more parts of the level because adding a few more enemies makes them all think slower (esp bad in dda). I recently had one where you had to use very smooth technique to escape from a pair of chaingun drones at the beginning, but then making the rest of the level utterly annihalated the puzzle.

Then, add more enemies. Not just more enemies for the sake of more enemies, no, just useful ones. Like a drone who has a chaingun and will move as an updated sentry if you get in his column, but will shoot you as he does that. He would never stop moving while shooting and each shot would pass through the same space he was aiming at from different angles, and he actvates the chase algo anytime. This would be the ultimate "don't let him chase you or ELSE" guy, not to mention the new toughest enemy.
Or a sentry that activates buttons, and then another who DEactivates buttons (closes doors back up, removes trapdoors). And obviously they use chase algo.
Or a "sticky drone" that makes you stick to it when it touches you and carries you along, in the same place relative to it, until a solid object (wall, door, 1 way wall, bounceblock) either peels you off or squishes you against it (if you are between the wall and it, its like riding a thwump up to the ceiling and not getting off in time). For a nice visual effect, if another enemy kills you your body will stick to it.
All of these could be useful for puzzle levels or specific goal levels. Lots of potential, and most of the coding's already there for different guys (the only new code would be the images, unpressing, and the sticky effect; the actions are there for different guys).

Alright, here's the deal. This text file includes two versions of a level: one with a missile turret, a guass gun (those two are easy), three thwumps and a buncha mines. It also has a few buttons.
The other has none of the above, with gold placed at regular intervals to reestablish the grid, and a coin where the missile turret and thwumps are.
Your goal is to, after viewing and probably playing the first level, go to the one without enemies and try to record a demo that works for the first level while playing the second. You must remember where the safe spots in the mine areas are, and where the buttons are and how to avoid the enemies; but you're doing it blind! Its pretty nervewracking by the time you get to the mines, and I was SOOO nervous when I got to the thwumps because I had no idea if I would/had made the jump at the right time. You'll see what I mean. The fact that you won't know about a mistake until you're done sure helps this atmosphere.

Of course, taken at face value, the level is unbelievably easy. But doing it blind is another story.

PS I included a demo made in the empty version. You can see I was pretty nervous in that top part.

is a puzzle game. In every sense. Quote: Kablizzy, Oct 9 2004, 02:31 AM
Map: Locks and Blocks
Author: Fox
Use of Tileset:8/10. I like what you did with the map, I think you manipulated it in a way that worked well. I didn't like the mass of mines, and I definitely don't like the chaingun drone with the bounce blocks. It takes a bit of luck to get through there without the drone shooting you up, and if the drone makes it out of the inner circle place, you're as good as screwed. N simply isn't fast enough to dodge a chaingun drone without some cover, and jumping down towards the goal, if the drone's in that area, there's nothing you can do but hope it misses.
Creativity:7/10. I think you did a decent burrito on placing things, and I kinda liked the mine right above the jump pads.
Fun:7/10. This map was really fun to play through, however, the chaingun drone, I disliked a bit.
Difficulty:7/10. It wasn't terribly difficult, but still, by no means balanced enough for me to think that it was perfect.
Excitement:5/10. It wasn't the most exciting of things, but it did flow fairly well. Once you trapped the first gauss turret, you have quite a while to sit and reflect on what path you'll take, and that slows things down a bit.
Other:3/5. I'ma give you three extra points on two things: First of all, for the good use of the jump pads, and secondly for having the gonads to put that chaingun drone where you did.
Total Score: 37

You do realise that one of the trapdoor buttons is there to trap the drone if you push it at the right time, but if you mess up the timing you're screwed. And am I the ONLY one who doesn't like the idea of a map where all of the already easy (aside from the chaingun) enemies can be completely deactivated but which can probably be done without? And the only one who doesn't get blocked isn't activated until the end and is lucky to get off one shot before you end the level.

#31862 11 2004-10-13T01:21:41Z brickman
Some person specific advice for tsuki on getting into soldat

Alright, tsuki, based on your forum personality, I think you would probably like to demolish your opponents with the M79 the most, out of the weapons, with chainsaw probably as a secondary. However, since the m79 is the hardest to learn to aim, I think you should start with an auto first. You wouldn't like the minimi because of its slowness or gun #2 (I forget the name) because you have to take a lot of pauses to reload, so you are left to choose between the very fast steyr and the more powerful but slower firing ak. I personally like the ak best, and liked #2 for a while because its small cooking wine unloaded very fast. I think you will dislike both the barret (sniper rifle) and those who use it, although you will hopefully opt for blowing their brains ouot instead of ragging on them. I can't imagine you camping.

I suggest you play a dm against bots with an auto weapon first to get used to the controlls, interface and aiming, then switch to the m79 and get used to it. Then jump right into an online ctf, and follow the first guy to leave your base using the upper route.

#1114 1 2004-10-15T22:29:41Z brickman
I have an idea that could serve multiple purposes. It would be elevator tiles.

Wait! Don't go.
These would be half full tiles (like type 5) with ropes leading to the ceiling to designate them as not normal floors. When you hit a switch it moves upwards until some part of it touches another tile (note: several of these next to each other count as one elevator). Once there it goes down until it hits something. While moving the switch does nothing (this is, as far as I can tell, the only thing we can do that would make a multiple use switch work, because if it was a door the game would open/close it every frame while n is on the switch. Also would work with drones flipping switches). Note that this does not necessarily squish n on the part of the elevator where tiles meet, since you could do two half iles that produce a full N height between. It moves at the same speed as a sentry drone, and its momentum is added to n's if he jumps on a moving platform.

These do produce several benifits. First, you can have creative puzzles where you must get the right combination of elevators. Or actually work a drone herding or "controll room" map into the real game (if they can flip switches). Or make interesting situations where you need the added height of an elevator in the "down" position to reach a platform, or perhaps even have to walljump off of one (still or moving), or climb onto a moving one. And the momentum thing leads to interesting timing levels, where you have to flip the switch and get across the map to land on the elevator before it meets you at the top so you can use its momentum for a jump. Etc.

#1132 1 2004-10-18T00:24:11Z brickman
I think that the timer being a requirement may be causing the player to be far more hasty than they should, and this takes away from the experience. Sure, it shows skill to quickly get through a level, but evading enemies is also important. But with a mandatory 90 second timer, and no way of knowing whether the next 4 levels will be gold filled cakewalks or long grueling ordeals, the message to the player is that stopping/wasting time is not allowed.
A perfect example of this is the level bore hunting (I forget the number). If you just wing it, the level is 97.9% impossible, because the laser drones will be in a position so that when you get onto a certain platform they already have the top of it covered in laser by the time you land. I spent forever trying it to no avail. Then, just for fun, I set the game to "practice mode" to play through the previous episodes again, and when I got to bore hunting I realised that if you just let the drones move for about 7 extra seconds, they will be on the wrong side of their platform when you get to the crucial part. It took me about 5 minutes to beat it then, and another 5 to win in normal mode. But under the pressure of a timer, the mere thought of wasting a good 7 seconds of your precious time is unthinkable. So you just muscle through it, or try to, and end up using less skill but more effort.
I think we need to change n to a points system. There is a "par time" for any given episode, and beating it grants you points for the time left. Getting gold also gives you both points and extra bonus time. Running out of time means no points for this level. There would still be a hard mode, which would be the origional n with slightly higher points as a reward.
Or at the very least, give each level its own time limit.

#32962 15 2004-10-22T01:36:27Z brickman
I think this is what n would look like if every level had been designed by Killisk. Insanely hard, requiring countless precision jumps, very long levels with no checkpoints, and few enemies. But its still very fun, I actually find the walljump system here to make more sense than n's (comon, even an uber ninja can't chimneyhop perfectly every time), although I dislike the skidjump and hate with a passion the fact that it doesn't care how hard/long you hit the jump key (in n, tapping shift doesn't make you go as high as slamming it down. Here, they both send you into that mine). But despite all its faults, this game excells over your typical platformer through creativity and level design. They are all extreemely clever, and I never would have expected the portable white platforms from part 5 to be a hindrance. All it needs are more checkpoints, and to not make it so that you can't unlock stuff while using them.

So far, I have gotten to 3-3 on normal and 5-something on easy (the first white block room). I initially just started the easy one so I could practice rooms using the checkpoint before conquering them in normal, but then realised that I was enjoying easy more than normal, so I let it pass the first game. I have all the gems from the first two areas in normal, but didn't bother collecting them in easy. Even with checkpoints, those rooms are too long!

Tax cuts that put ANY money back in the hands of the wealthy are bad. Here's why:
Lets say that it costs $100 a month for a family to have food, and 300 for rent (these are example figures). Now, family A makes $800 a month, and family B makes $450. Now, if each is taxed 20%, then at the end of the month Family A has $240 discretionary income, after food shelter and taxes. Family B $40 in debt after just just the essentials. Sure, they pay a portion of what they make, but the numbers don't work.

Well, personally I think that individuals voting Nader or Badnarik or whoever are useless. The same part of me that detests major religion says that doing something that you know for a fact will be shot down and be a wasted effort instead of doing something which you think will make things better, though obviously not perfect, just due to principle is dumb. If Nader is better than Kerry and Kerry is better than Bush, then I'll vote Kerry because I know that a vote for Nader doesn't do much. Now, if you could somehow persuade a large group of people who both use a similar logic structure (with Kerry and Bush switched half the time) to all pull together, and convince them that if they all vote for their candidate then the votes cancel out but if they all vote for a third party then they make a difference, THAT is worthwhile. I firmly believe that all we need to do to jump start our legal system and whip it into shape is for a third party to win just ONE ELECTORAL VOTE (technically, you can't win less than three, but thats off topic) from ONE STATE in ONE ELECTION. Because that would send a message to every person in America, from the far left to the far right, from California to the New York Island, that third parties are not a joke, and that there is another viable option. And while at first only one new party would exist, two election cycles later the weakened barrier would be broken and all the candidates would get their names in the papers, and we would have 8 way debates and never have to choose between dumb and dumber again.

My dad says that third parties already serve a subtle purpose. He says that if a third party gets a relatively high % in polls (3% is relatively high for thirdies), the two main contenders see that those views are popular and will both begin to incorporate them into their campaign. Thus, as long as campaign promises have some factual base, third parties effect what happens when they become popular (and if there's no base, there's no democracy).

#35141 203 2004-11-03T22:46:23Z brickman
I think I'm going to PM tsukatu to come here and decide once and for all whether these maps are as bad as we say. Also, as for the scale, I think that giving a lot of scores above 40 is even worse than giving low scores. And I've seen a lot of scores>40 in these contests. I think that there are maps deserving less than ten here. And as for the unnecessary aggression in comments, which does exist a little but not as much as you make it out to be, if I say "the one jump was too hard" or "the enemies didn't pose much threat", I gaurantee that I would get back "is that really bad enough for a 3?" So I try to let the comments express the severity of the problem, which sadly is strong more often than not. The only ones which I suppose are really questionable are the comments that went along with 0s, but that was because a comment fully explaining what was wrong would take up more space than this whole post.
The way I judged this contest was this: I made a standard with the first map which obeyed the rules (symetry), and maybe one or two after it. I planned to judge other maps in a way so that the scores were all relative. Thus is map a had 23 and map b was worse, it would have less than 23 points, with the difference depending on how much worse. And visa versa. This ingenous system was designed to make sure that standards for judging didn't gradually change as the contest went on, with a map that was better than most scoring better than another which was better than it because at the time the first appeared I had nothing to compare it too. Or visa versa. I wanted a system where maps were comnpared to those that already had scores, instead of arbitrary numbers that might vary by the number of crap/good maps or the mood of the reviewer.
This was an excellent plan except it had one fatal flaw: poor overall quality of maps.
When I set the standard (really symetry was pretty much the starting point for the standard), I was expecting that, like in ned 2, the maps would get better after the first week. Go check that thread, the earlier maps all scored lower because they weren't as good, and I figured the same would happen (especialy since there were only three maps when I set the scoring standard, and only one which qualified, the potential good ideas hadn't been tapped yet). But for some odd reason, this season something went wrong. People started submitting crappy maps continously, or at least poor maps (the really crappy ones weren't too common). Also, the scoring system gave a full %40 of the score to having a good, well used and unique theme, but people wrongly interpreted it as just having a theme of some kind somewhere within the map. And so by my system, and because by the time I realised that the maps weren't getting better I had already scored too many to change the scale, I began rating them lower than or slightly higher than 26, which was the standard I had set out at the start. By the time complaints began pouring in I had begun trying to use the maps in general as my scale instead of just the first few, but I could not change it enough to make people happy without making the previous scores worthless. I can not determine the quality of the maps, I can only express the quality, and quality maps were not able to balance the low quality maps. Thus, the scores became generally low.
I will say, however, that most or all of the maps with a single digit score fully deserve it.

I suppose this could all be avoided by waiting until the contest was half over before starting to judge, but that carries its own problems. The maps pour in with no feedback, so until the judges start people have to guess at what we want. They recieve no feedback and thus don't know what was wrong, and repeat the same mistakes again and again. Thus, waiting to judge actually does make the maps worse than if you offer feedback all throughout. But it decreases the quality of the scores proportionately, a problem which I had thought I had solved back in the first paragraph. And of course there's always the issue of judging all those maps after that many have accumulated, which by my logic leads to bulk reviews which have lower quality. I guess my logic was flawrd.

Well, I think a lot of games give a reward for playing. RTSs give you access to the bad guy, for example (if they're any good).
An even better example is Castlevania: Circle of the Moon for GBA. Beating it gives you a special name, and entering that name gives you magician mode, where you start with all the cards for spells (the last few you can't even GET in normal unless you go into the insanely hard arena and are lucky enough that the one room with dark and light armors someone drops them) and your stats are altered to give you lots of magic but be weak (mp and int start and go up about four times as fast, but str, def, and hp suffer greatly). Its a different game, but thats not all: beating magician mode gives you fighter mode, where you have high hp, high str, high def, and no spells, and you end up getting far in the game faster due to your strength without having to level up a lot so that by the time things start getting hard your physical attributes are very strong but your luck is poor and you get few items. Then there's shooter mode, where you ahve slightly worse physical stats than normal mode but subweapons do huge damage and yuo can get guided knives. Then there's thief mode, the one that gets you through the gae fastest, where you have the same stats as shooter except you have 1600 luck at the start and collect items off the bat faster than others do at the end of the game.
You could also consider story sequences an unlockable.
Seriously, there's no excuse not to make something decent at the end of a game. So what if only a few people get it, they earned it!

#37487 31 2004-11-22T21:39:47Z brickman
Look at game you're talking about. It includes a whopping 8 different enemies (including mines), three types of door (none of which are reusable), tiles, two non-tile or door objects that you can touch without dying, and one collectible. And thats it. Nothing else. Its little wonder that people found new uses for old items. they had to. You can only go so long with that limited an object set. So you start finding new tricks, undocumented uses for the existing items. You can make a moving wall, you can make a stronger launchpad, you can teleport (Not that I want teleports in, they're an example), you can make a level that plays itself. You can screw with a one-way (no, I don't liek that either), you can make a small space that requires momentum to get through, you can make delayed mines and buttons (sadly, they may not work too well what with the timer), you can give n momentum by almost squishing him and thus shooting him out. Most of the useful tricks are well-known enough that the majority of players know about them already, and you can figure them out anyways (there's always the help thing if its too hard). And it adds variety.
I cannot think of another good game like n. I don't mean one that plays like n, I can think of two very similar ones off the top of my head which are very good. I mean a game which limits itself to only the objects found within the first few levels. Where over the course of the entire game you never see something new. No powerups (or downs), no conveyor belts, no water, no bosses, no scrolling levels, no moving laser beams or huge banks of switches, no tnt, no drills. No moving platforms, no gears, no pressure plates, no secret walls. And it has 6 times the number of levels in the two other games I was thinking of combined! At that point you have to ask yourself two questions: How did it work, and how much longer can it work? And if you don't allow creative uses of the current items (not even necessarily new ones, but new uses of oldies) then the answer to the second question is not much longer. You have to let the game evolve.

#37719 27 2004-11-24T17:34:19Z brickman
Except for telling the game which sprite, which way its facing, nd what its rotation is. Remember, the way flash works, n running up a slope is the same sprite as n running on flat ground, only rotated (thats why they chose flash), and when he runs the other way its the same sprite but flipped, so a minimum of three extra things for it to check (sprite, rotation, left or right) in addition to his exact coordinates. Vs with a dot, its only one sprite which needs no flipping or rotating, thus only coords must be checked each frame.

I somehow don't think this rating system means anything. Not the way it is now. When you're given 3000 things you COULD rate, and not encouraged to rate any of them, then typically only the ones at the extreems will be rated, and any maps whose average score is between 1.5 and 4 is not likely to get enough votes to even have a rating. I currently have no rated maps, thus am automatically at the bottom of the top rated list. The limited 10-5 scale doesn't help either-- it has no degrees of goodness, just "best" "good" "average" "poor" "very bad"and "donkey shit." A ten point system is much more logical. Additionally, people can see that a map has a 4 after 5 votes, and say "I think it should be a three," but instead of of rating it 3 he rates it 0 to bring the aerage down to three all at once, by himself, thus making the entire thing a useless system. Also, there's not enough rated maps for "top rated" to mean anything: there's a guy with an average rating of 0 halfway up on the first page of authors, and there's good people (like me) who have no rated maps under HIM on the top rated list. And last time I checked, the first page of "top" rated maps dipped into the "poor" range, possibly even the "very bad" range.

Revamp the system or scrap it, its useless now.

#37884 18 2004-11-25T22:25:04Z brickman
The two people were me and Eli, because you had said that you would "mabey" join depending on who ran it, and thus I couldn't count on you as a third member. I suppose that three is enough, and I'll let Tsuki start it (thus, whatever setting you want). We probably need some rules just to be safe, so I'm gonna start a list and Tsukatu or Eli or anyone else can add to it as they see fit:

1) Unless the setting Tsukatu happens to be feudal Japan, you may not have a ninja as a character. Nor will there be any robots, homing missiles, thwumps, or anything else from n. Except of course gold, but it will not float or extend your lifespan--its just currency.
2) No super powerful characters. I'm fine with you being a general or lmage or something like that, and if your person can win a three on one fight when given proper equipment, thats fine, but you can't take down 20 armored knights by yourself (under normal circumstances) and you can't throw fireballs bigger than your house.
3) Try to avoid making things happen to another person's character that they would not want. I'm not saying that they're invincible while you're posting, but you can't have Eli's arm bitten off without his Out of Character consent, because that screws up the roleplay somewhat. Use your judgement, and ask yourself whether thats a decision that they would want to make were it your character. Absolutely no killing another character without permission.
4) As an extension of the above rule, try to control other people's characters as little as possible. If you need to do minor things, then describing what they're doing (a fight starts, you can say that he pulls out his sword and begins attacking the foes) or providing simple conversation responses (name, greeting, explaining what happened), but keep it to a minimum. Try not to do anything that would be out of character for them.
5) Npcs may be controlled, to a dgree, by any participant, but make them act like they would be acting. If an npc is tied to a character (ie another man from a sodiers scattered company), he is allowed a little more controll of that npc.
6) Don't try to ruin the rp, even if what you're doing isn't against an above rule, you will have your posts deleted by Tsukatu very quickly if you do something that you know is hurting the rp (I say Tsukatu will edit it because he's the only mod we have on board at this point).

Aside from #1, these rules all come from other forum rps, and they work pretty well. Feel free to add to or alter them , even do it in this post if you want Tsuki (of course Eli doesn't have that option).

#37990 52 2004-11-26T15:37:17Z brickman
Here's my logic:

A drunk driver is very likely to kill someone every time he does it. The other person is %100 innocent, and loses his whole F***ing life.
A law is passed that prevents John Doe from getting his after work drink. He lives within 5 minutes walking distance of both the bar and hs job, so he never actually has to drive after getting his one bottle. He is somewhat inncoent--he probably isn't gonna hurt someone, but he's still injesting a chemical that makes you stupid-- and he loses: his beer. Not his job, not his food, not his health, just beer. Even if its his crutch he uses to deal with his dead-end job, he now has extra money in his pocket thats not being spent on alcohol, so maybe he can afford to look for a healthier way of dealing with it.

Of course, we aren't talking about prohibition. We already saw that there's too many stupid alcoholics for that. But limiting alcohol, or holding you accountable after you drink--thats important. Maybe a law mandating that breathalizers (devices that require you to breath into them and won't let you start the car if it detects any alcohol) be in every car would help. It definitely makes more sense than a seatbelt law, because sane people would want a car with seatbelts more than one without anyways, so it doesn't really need a law, but this one helps save lives outside of the vehicle its in as well as inside.
Yeah, maybe we don't enforce all of our laws enough, but that doesn't mean make fewer laws. That just means that we can't take someone in if we catch them doing something we know is wrong because its no longer illegal so they end up walking. It means more effective enforcement. Compare it to an empire: it may not be practical for one man to rule a huge empire, but that doesn't mean he gives some of it back, does it? No, it means that he makes a system of lower level nobles to rule the various areas who all answer to him, because a more efficient system makes it possible to govern a whole continent if you need to.

#38943 120 2004-12-01T21:44:23Z brickman
My view on dwarves in this rp:
The dwarves are the industrious race, and they hold all the cards in rescource economics because all the mines are under their control. Selling metals and putting taxes on them is where most of their money comes from, and their power. They also hold a monopoly on quality modernized goods: only a fool would use a rifle not made by dwarves for fear of losing an arm, and seige equipment all comes from them. They basically are the race who rns warfare, because if you can't trade with the dwarves you can't make or purchase any of the tools of war and end up with an army consisting entirely of archers clad in leather, since those are the only things you don't need metal for.
Incidentally, the elves (eternal enemies of dwarves) are all archers and spearmen and the gnomes (eternal friends of the dwarves because of their contributions to dwarven technology) almost never have to fear war with anyone but the elves, because noone wants to be cut off from the dwarves. And the dwarves themselves, despite being fairly incompetent with any non-black powder weapons (and not exactly marksmen with blackpowder ones) never have to worry about war, because any army pitted against them would be unable to supply itself with even so much as a short sword per man or any of the equipment needed to breach the walls around the dwarven cities/mines.

As for naming the other races:
Slitheraki for the lizards, manticore for the snakes, and they are definitely on the same side (aka evil).

#38959 123 2004-12-01T22:28:04Z brickman
Hmm, dwarves as the dominant race, that could work.

Anyways, the only thing holding them in check is the elves. The elves hate the dwarves to the point of open war because they destroy the forest to make new mines and to fuel their massive war engines (they use all the coal from their mines in furnaces, so the war engnes require other fuels and wood is a useful choice). They believe their purpose is to protect the forests, so they long ago shunned the dwarves and learned to make bows and spears from wood, which is in even more abundant supply to them than metal is to dwarves. A singe fallen tree can supply a dozen elfish warriors with their equipment (for this reason, they allowed these secrets to be revealed to other races in hopes of reducing the dependence on the dwarves). When the dwarves began to impede upon the forest during a temporary low in the economy (their current mines were running dry) the elves declared that they would war with the dwarves until they left. The dwarvish technologies developed quickly as new mines were founded and the economy picked back up, and they quickly became dependent on large quantities of wood and minerals, meaning that they could not leave the forest without plunging their race into a dark age.
So they had no choice but to continue to expand into the forests, and the elves had no choice but to try to halt their development. Even with their allies the armell, a race like elves but without the connection to nature and thus without their skill with bows and spears, they could never crush the elfish resistance, and the constant war with elfkind is the only reason that the dwarves have not been able to seize full control of the continent. They must constantly train dwarves to fight with their own technologies, and due to their lack of skill with conventional weaponry (which is much easier to produce then guns) they are forced to constantly hire mercenaries and maintain close allies (gnomes and armell). These expenses cut from their treasury so much that they cannot afford to conquer any new territory, only continue to fight the elves and expand their mines into the forests. Almost all non-elf races rely on dwarfish metal, so they have coeerced almost every civilized race to war with the elves as well and elves are killed on sight by most people. Still, the elves breed like rabbits and have a near-infinite supply of the resources they use, as well as unmatched knowledge of their forests, and thus they cannot be wiped out. They have learned to kill humans and other allies of the dwarves upon contact, knowing that they will do the same, although its rumored that some humans have actually allied themselves wtih these forestfolk and become druids, with forest lore almost equal to that of the elves and the ability to mix seemingly useless herbs and plants into elixirs granting healing or speed.
Armell were the result of crossbreeding (for lack of a better term) between dwarves and elves, before the great war had started, and allied themselves with dwarves because they were much less suited than elves for a non-metal society, and because they did not wish to have their thriving trade economy cut off (which it would be if they had allied themselves with the elves at the time of the split). The forests controlled by them are not the same as the forests of the elves, because the forests near dwarfish mines grant them enough forces from their allies that they can push out the elves from just those parts.

You may discard any parts that you don't think hood, and I suppose a little rearrangement of elf/armell cities would be needed, but you can't say thats not an interesting (and detailed) backstory.

And yes, that means you can't be an elf.

#39032 130 2004-12-02T04:30:33Z brickman
Okay, I hate to inform you that you're the only one poking holes so far.

This is a work of fiction. You could say that any typ of monopoly in our capitolist society would be doomed from the start by that logic, but with just one or two different election results we could still have one phone company (making a killing), one railroad company (makinga killing, at least as long as trains were important), one oil company (making a killing), and one. . .
Well, you get the point. People get monopolies by driving out the competition, whether through force (and/or suoperior resources) or through superior marketing strategy, and then as long as its something people need they can do anything they want with it. If standard phone company suspects you of splicing a phone line, you're never gonna be able o use your phone again, so that spliced chord isn't doing you much good, is it?
And I didn't mean they don't know how to dig a shiny gem out of the ground. I meant they lost the knowledge of how to identify and refine useful metals, such ass irons, and other important things like coal (if you can't recognize coal, you can't make too many bars of refined metal, can you?). And as for bows: would you believe that a bow is not as obvious to someone who doeesn't already know about it as, say, a sword? See, with your typical weapon, you just have a sharp edge or a heavy club and that causes direct physical harm. With a bow, you take a slightly curved piece of wood, tie a special string to it, make a little arrow, put the arrow between stick and string, pull back, and the string magically sends that arrow flying. Thats a lot more complicated than "if this end touches you, you bleed". I'm sure that it took every civilized ancient race 2 years to invent such a weapon. Not! One invented it, then they used it on someone else, then they realized it would work and set about figuring out how to make it, then they use it on someone else and. . . they did not all independently think up the bow.
And as for a weapon thats been made being put into circulation: there's lots of things that can happen to a weapon. It breaks. It rusts. The elements damage it. The guy carrying it gets slain by a wild animal. A guy drops it while fleeing. And there's always the fact that the population is growing, and thus the army is growing, and thus they need more swords. Blacksmiths had a lot of job security in midevil times, and so did miners (well, the individual miner didn't, but the industry of mining was in demand for more than a few years).
The thing about dwarf fighting skills: I may have not held it to the same degree the whole time, but the bottom line was that when dwarves are at war they don't like using swords and axes.

And finally, to number 1: the idea is that this is not DnD, but most rpgs mimic it a lot more than this one. If dwarves in DnD were like the elves are and elves were like the dwarves are, the current system would sound just as silly. Its just not what you're used to, its not the same-old same-old that most rpgs are saturated with.

#39140 136 2004-12-02T22:22:20Z brickman
The thing is, if the elves aren't challenging the dwarves, then we are left with the origional problem suki had presented, namely: why don't the dwarves control everything yet?
And as for monopolizing the metal industry: you must remember that although mining may not be hard to figure out when you notice that there's a bed of nice shiny crystals under your farm, ores and other minerals are not as simple as just digging and pulling it out of the ground. You must first know how to find and identify deposits of useful stuff, then must learn to sort out the different types of metal (if you mix copper and iron, I gaurantee you that what you get is useless), and then how to refine them. And even if people are smart enough to tell iron ore from normal rock and dig it all out, they still need a furnace to melt it into bars, which would then be useful for making stuff in a forge. That first furnace has to be a lot hotter than the blacksmith's one, though, because the stuff needs to be melted instead of softened, and that requires lots of coal. And coal, in case you didn't know, looks remarkably like ordinary rock. Why, its a wonder that people ever even figured out how to make stuff from metal in the real world, with no knowledge and no assurance that what they were trying for wasd possible, or even what they were trying for. Thus, I can see it being very feasible that humans would lose the ability to find the ores and turn them into useable metal bars, by this string of events:
1) dwarvish metal is cheaper than human metal. 2) smiths all decide to buy their metal from dwarves, because its cheaper. 3) forges run by humans go broke and close down. 4) dwarves stop buying ore from human miners, so they go broke. 5) now all mining and refining of ore by humans has been ended, and the dwarves are free to raise the prices (after a waiting period to make sure the venture isn't wasted). They thought in the long term, we thought short-term, we lost out.

Okay. I am Sir Relnor, a knight in the port town of Aled, one of the only two residing in that small city to protect it from the lizards. With the recent raids, all ports had been assigned knights to prevent the possibility of losing it to the Szarzina. In the past month, none of the weekly shipments coming from the southeast have arrived, and the ships sent to investigate reported that the lighthouse, which is always kept brightly lit, is unlit, and additionally the docks themselves had been destroyed. It would be unsafe to try to dock there. Fearing for the worst, a council was held where it was quickly decided that a convoy should be sent to try to find out what happened and fix it. The party would have to visit with the dwarves and armell to purchase the supplies needed to repair the damages, and Aled was the closest town to their lands. Thus the people to make the trip all went there to assemble. By the time they were all assembled, there were 10 soldiers, an archer, and a dozen workers who would be able to perform any repairs needed, not to mention the gold and goods needed for the dwarves and Armel. Sadly, Sir Mordak, the knight they had chosen to lead the expidition, had fallen deathly ill while on route to Aled. They could not afford to delay long enough to send another, so Sir Relnor was chosen to lead the group in his stead. He set out to the north, towards the dwarven mountains. . .

I am Sir Relnor, a knight in the port town of Aled, of about ten assigned to protect it from the Naga. With the recent raids, all ports had been assigned knights to prevent the possibility of losing them to the Naga. In the past month, none of the weekly shipments coming from the southeast have arrived, and the ships sent to investigate reported that the lighthouse, which is always kept brightly lit even during day, is unlit, and additionally the docks themselves had been destroyed. It would be unsafe to try to dock there. Fearing for the worst, a council was held where it was quickly decided that a convoy should be sent to try to find out what happened and fix it. The party would have to visit with the dwarves and armell to purchase the supplies needed to repair the damages, and Aled was the closest town to their lands. Thus the people to make the trip all went there to assemble. By the time they were all assembled, there were 10 soldiers, an archer, and a dozen workers who would be able to perform any repairs needed, not to mention the gold and goods needed for the dwarves and Armel. Sadly, Sir Mordak, the knight they had chosen to lead the expidition, had fallen deathly ill while on route to Aled. They could not afford to delay long enough to send another, so Sir Relnor was chosen to lead the group in his stead. He set out to the north, towards the dwarven mountains. . .

#39821 16 2004-12-06T21:59:45Z brickman
Thadmir, one of the guards on the first shift, struggled to stay awake. He stared out into the darkness, thinking he had spotted movement. But how could he, with darkness like this. He looked over at his partner, noticed him drifting to sleep.
"Stay awake. Our shift is still another to hours, you'll get to sleep then."
Bordak's eyes opened slightly, and he grogily spoke. "Why bother? There's nothing out there, you know that. We're perfectly safe. Nothing's. . . gonna. . ." his eyelids slid closed.
"Bordak!" He did not stir, and so Thadmir got up to shake him awake. . . but he never made it. A bone club landed a blow on his head, and his body fell limp. Bordak still did not stir.
The naga leader hissed to the others. "We have the element of surprise. Kill them quietly, we do not wish to wake the whole group."
The snakemen hurried past the guard towards the tents, in which slept the entire expidition. Bordak stirred. Half asleep, without opening his eyes, he murmured "Come on, Thadmir. There's absolutely no naga in these hills. Let me close my eyes, I'll only be a minute." The naga stopped, turned towards him.
"He is still asleep" said the leader, the only one in the group who could understand human tounge. The others hissed "Lets kill him before he awakes then!" Before the chief could respond, one of them had already clubbed Bordak. Unfortunately, Bordak had shifted in his sleep, and the blow did not kill him. It did, however, wake him.
"OW! I was only out for a moment, I was resting my--what in the world--augghhhhhhhh!" he cried as the naga finished the job, crushing his skull with his club. The cry peirced the night, and immediately every soldier in the caravan was on his feet with weapon in hand.
"Curse you, you woke them. Now we must hide!"
By the time the soldiers had reached the clearing, the naga were gone from sight. "Come out, fiends" cried one of the soldiers, and immediately the creatures obeyed: 15 naga came pouring out of the hills on all sides, surrounding the men. They did not need any orders, the men instinctively backed into the middle of the circle and fought off the snakes. The men were all highly trained, and had equipment of steel to math the bone clubs of the enemy, and by the end of the battle there lay 14 naga and only two humans, and they was down before the battle begun.
One of the two stirred. "He's still alive, quickly, help him up!" Two soldiers rushed over to help up Thadmir, and he opened his mouth. "I tried to tell him. . .could not afford to let sleep claim us, that . . . danger present. . . didn't listen. . . ambush. . . my head. . ." and he drifted out of consciousness. Relnor's shouted "Come on men, we may not have lost him. Get him to a tent!" And he thought silently how could we forget to bring a medic? There's no way we could be expected to make such a journey without a medic. I could lose my rank for this. I only hope that we can secure a medic in Markio.

"What is it sir?"

Tell them that the lizards are seiging the dwarven town of Morid at this very moment, and that they should send any and all available soldiers there to help defend it. Warn them not to completely abandon the capitol, however, because it seems almost certain that this attack force would have to have attacked via sea in the Vinara Ocean, meaning they could easily attack any coastal town near that area." Then, as Valdvir rushed off, Relnor addressed the troops in general. "Boys, we're turning back. Its no longer a caravan per say. See, there were only three wagons to start with in order to be allowed to pass through the elven forests, and two of those wagons are still going to Fellos, meaning that only one wagon is moving towards Morid.

With only rations and soldiers to worry about, the wagon moved at a speed almost three times what it had when they had to deal with the repair supplies and the workers. By nightfall, they were within a mile of Morid. They didn't dare stop to rest, however, knowing the seige was going on as they went. An hour later, they were just within sight of the walls of Morid. They could see dwarves with crossbows and pistols shooting from parapets as lizardmen hurled huge bone javelins with amazing strength. They had to have inhuman strength, because the javelins were going over the walls so large they had never been breached, and not even the elves with their bows had ever been able to kill a dwarf on the parapets. There must have been over a hundred dwarves, but there seemed to be less than half that number of lizardmen. Some of them tried to hurl grappling hooks onto the walls, but the dwarven parapets had been designed specifically to not allow grappling hooks and ladders to take hold. Sir Relnor watched as one of the lizards recieved a shot to his right arm, which held a spear, and still tossed it with force enough to spit the dwarf who had hit him.
Sir Relnor then spotted the mast of a docked imperial ship, a sign that the emperor had sent help. But no human bodies were on the battlefield, meaning that they had not yet arrived. He scanned the hills, and then spotted the banner of an imperial platoon. They were preparing to ambush, apparently waiting for an oppurtunity to show themselves. He then spotted another banner 40 feet away, and the signal was sent with a raising of that banner. Both groups charged forward, with fierce battle cries as they clashed swords against spears. . . then the men of sir Relnor's company shot forward as well, without the noise.

#42291 134 2004-12-24T15:21:23Z brickman
Hey I thought of two new ideas to help strengthen your voting system. First, as a way to help prevent people like captain donut, you may not vote unless the account that is casting the vote has made at least one map. Of course, they COULD still do it, but it would be much harder to do and much easier to spot and stop.

Second, and a bit less unrefutable, make the vote averaging cut out the highest and lowest vote. This is a system designed to ensure that one person liking/hating a map doesn't by itself add or drop a ninja or two. Maps currently rated very high/low will probably be mostly unaffected (maybe even drift farther towards their extreem), but maps in the middle range will reflect the opinion of the general public a bit better.
Lets take a hypothetical example. This would NEVER happen. Lets say that Maximo makes a super DDA, and eight people watch it. All of them like it, but one believes that the way to get his maps to the top is by sendingg better maps to the botom, so votes for the map are: 5, 4, 5, 5, 4, 4, 5, 0. Now, before that 0 the average was just above 4.5, and after it the score is: 4. The map lot an entire half ninja from one person. This shatters the map as far as the top rated map and author lists go. But, with high/low averaging, the score becomes exactly 4.5. Its dropped slightly (a seventh of a ninja) from what it was before the 0, but i still accurately reflects what the majority of people think. The vote of one cannot very easily shake the votes of many. This also encourages people to vote accurately instead of "Well, the average is 4, I think its a three, so I'll rate it 0 to lower the average to 3." It works both ways, so that if I see my friend's map is floundering I can't give it a huge boost.

#43754 33 2005-01-01T19:49:32Z brickman
I've figured out one big facet of the system. Specifically, I've determined that the reason I kept getting frustrated in later levels was becasue the bottom of the boss was growing so fast that by the 8th boss I would have about 1.5 cubic centimeters to work with most of the time due to his bulk, while being attacked with lasers, mass ammounts of cannonballs--the works. Dodging is one thing, but dodging in a space roughly twice the size of your ship is not fun. So I figured out that since the order in which you attack sides of the ship determines the growth, attacking the front first is suicide. You can only hope to survive by always going for the pieces in the upper corners (upper left and upper right) first, aggressively stomping them out first. That way, he grows outwards instead of downwards, and by level ten you still have enough room to dodge all the crap he's throwing at you. Even with a false start, I was able to get farther doing that than I had doing it normally.

Edit: I'm attaching a demo. Noone should ever be expected to dodge that many cannonballs. Ever.

#44991 34 2005-01-09T02:29:32Z brickman
No, avernum is the opposite of Morrowwind in every aspect that I factually know about Morrowwind. Its single player with a party of up to four people (even though conversation and stuff seems to act like 3 of the people are mute), turn based combat with action points, you gain levels so that you can amass skillpoints to give to any skill you wish (aka you can have 10 alchemy and 10 bow skill without ever doing anything except bash stuff with a hammer, if thats how you want to place the points, and doing stuff like potion making or first aid doesn't grant xp), there's a lot of npc quests of various sizes (from stealing something from one of the shipments from the surface to clearing out a fort full of lizard people to retrieve a magic amulet for the mayor), its got a weell crafted plot (which, sadly, we won't be able to go through in our rp), four installments, and the biggest munchkin things are tricking people to leave the room so you can rob them blind and sell everything back, and giving every person in your party a starting magic level of 5 or more because mages (and especially ice lances) are vastly overpowered. Actually, that second one doesn't work in parts 3 or 4 (not sure about 2, I haven't played in too long). And its shareware, but I never registered and still got as much out of it as in most full games, including the full plot (since it summarizes what happened in the previous one at the start of each game). I could talk longer, but I applaud you if you're still reading now.

The point is, its not Morrowind, and you can play Avernum enough to be able to participate in an rp for free, and more, and its such a good game I doubt rpg fans will be able to stop until they run out of free territory to explore and clear of monsters/valluables. It doesn't suck up your life like an online rpg though, so there's no real reason that anyone who wants to shouldn't try it. The only thing we would have to decide is which time we would set our rp in. I suggest the first, because in part 2 and 3 chances are our party wouldn't be in the area where the most real game takes place, and 4 lacks any substantial setting at all (for that matter, 4 lacks almost every good quality of the others). I definitely say we shouldn't be the heros of the actual games, because we already know that plot.

Edit: silly me. Spiderweb Software. Thats where you can download the Avernun series free areas, Exile series free areas (same plot as avernum, only done with inferior technology, fewer quests, no joining the party, and in my opinion a MUCH better, though still a bit unbalanced, magic system), Geneforge free parts (may just be me, but I think the better graphics are balanced out by poorer gameplay here), and a few other shareware "demos". Everyone should check it out, they even have a thing or two for non-rpg fans. Everything there is quality, but don't expect fancy particle effects or advanced physics systems or any other technical showcasings.

Double edit: whoa, I sure do talk a lot whenever I'm talking about other games.

First, go borrow some patience. You seem to lack it, but you will need it in this and future endeavors.
Then, go into ned. If you want it to go right, all you have to do is place it halfway into a wall, making sure that if said wall is not the border there's not an empty tile on the other side. If you want it going up, down, or left, you must turn gridlock off and precisely place it just off the grid (I neither understand nnor can stand this, but thats how it is), via trial and error, and you now have one. I suggest, if you aren't excessively patient, you search for a map called "N juice" or "claustrophobia" (don't blame me if thats the wrong name), where many are already set up, then delete the tileset and objects and go off of those thwmps. #45553 3 2005-01-11T21:48:01Z brickman
Gold: I don't always add gold, although when I think about it I suppopse I should. The fact of the matter is, people have different levels of skill. A map thats very hard for one person may be of medium difficulty to another, and nigh-impossible for a third. Gold allows you to appeal to more of those people. People who can hardly beat the level ignore the gold and get a challenge thats reasonable for them, and then a slightly more skilled player will go in and grab some of the gold, going a little out of their way but not being able to take it all. Then a great player comes in and gets all the gold. These players each was treated to just the right ammount of difficulty, because the difficulty is variable depending on how much gold they're willing to go for. Without the gold, one would be satisfied and the other two would say its too hard/easy. Of course, gold is a bad thing when it is too easy to get. If going for the gold doesn't add challenge, then yes, its not needed. But it usually is.

Difficulty: once again, different skill levels. There are people who can beat almost any non-broken map on numa with enough effort, hereafter referred to as the uber-players. Some people, especially the uber-players themselves, make maps intended mostly for them. If you play those maps, you will fail miserably, because it wasn't for you. Meanwhile, there are poor players who can only beat a handful of maps. Many people, often those same people, make maps suited to them. If you play those maps, you will finish and say "wtf, what's the point? Its too easy". And you're right, because it wasn't made for you. Then, there are intermediate players, like you and me, and maps made for us, once again often by us. These range from pretty easy to pretty hard. Actually, there's a range in all three categories, but the intermediate is where its biggest. Each particular person has a certain difficulty "niche", a perfect difficulty, but its not likely that they will ever find more maps at that exact difficulty than can be counted on their fingers. Most will be off, by either a little or a lot. No map is the right difficulty for all people.

So then, why rate on difficulty? Unless its a three-second long map where you only need to make one jump to win, a map thats physically impossible, or a survival map with an easy infinity loop, difficulty is not a judge of how good a map is or whether others will like it. The only ones who I think have any right to say whats too hard are the top players, and unless you're one of them, don't.

If Imir hadn't used up all of their oil when killing the guards, they might be able to throw it off the back and create a fire to slow the attackers, but he had thrown the whole flask. . .

Then an idea occurred to him. It was a longshot, but he had no choice. He yelled to one of the troops to take his place, and he leaped across the small gaps between the clustered ships and over to the one in the back, where Detario was. He was busy picking off attackers with his standard dwarven pistol--none of the shots pierced their scaly hides, but the force was enough to knock them off their small boats and into the water, where they were as good as dead.
"Quickly,do you know how to dissamble that thing?"
He pulled the trigger, and a lizard on a raft is knocked back into the water, then began reloading.
"Yes, but why would I want to do that? I am having a hard enough time holding them off already. . ."
"The sparker in there. We need it. None of our cannons can be pointed backwards, but there's lots of gunpowder for them. Its a longshot, but if we toss a barrel of gunpowder over the side and you hit it with a spark, it could make an explosion that would take out the approaching raiders."
"But that would take out our ships as well. . ." With a lactose intolerant, another lizard dropped from a fishing boat. They were getting closer, and would be able to board in less than 5 minutes, and there were far too many to pick them all off. "Wait, we don't have to use the sparker. We can make a fuse out of any length of rope. . ."
"That's an excellent idea." Without another word, relnor was off, and came back with another man carrying a barrel of blackpowder. He also had a meter long rope, the end of which he stuck in the barrel. He lit the end, and threw the barrel off. The fuse was about ten seconds long, with the marauders only feet away from the ship. With a cry, the four on the farthest back boat lept onto another one, and stayed down as an explosion opened a gaping hole in the boat only a second after the last one had jumped. The radius was small enough that the other 5 were unharmed. As the smoke cleared, they looked over the scene. . . and saw the lizards fleeing. The explosion had shaken them, and they knew there was more where that had come from, and longer ropes so that the defenders would not have to damage their own boats as well. There was no hope of taking these boats, especially not in their small crafts, and the lizards were not fond of their navy either. They had been bested for now. . . but Relnor noticed that as their sails shrunk towards the horizons, they began cahnging directions, splitting left and right. As they faded into the mists, Relnor was sure they were not done yet. They were going to make another attack, an ambush from both sides. He turned to Valdvir, once again by hi side. "We have to get out of these boats. FAST. Go east. We'll never make it to Kruzano, we have to abandon the ships on the coastline. In fact. . . maybe we could set up a trap for those lizards once they find them. . ."
Valdvir raised the cry. "Head east, head for land. Don't hold the course for Kurzano, head for the open shoreline."

#1890 1 2005-01-24T21:44:10Z brickman
So I was searching around on gamehippo, looking for something to occupy my weekend, and I stumbled upon this. I am posting to the description game because, sadly, there's some Japaneese filename issues that require a patch linked to in that description, or Japanese language support, and unfortunately that patch doesn't work on some computers (sorry for wasting your time if it doesn't for you). In the game, you control a ghost who can take control of any enemy (well, any enemy that isn't a turret or a boss) by jumping on it and pressing z and possess it to do his bidding until it dies or he discards it by pressing c. Either one removes the enemy and reverts Obake to ghost form. While in control of an enemy only the enemy takes damage, not Obake himself, but they usually go down pretty quick if you aren't careful and its not always easy to get another host. While controlling an enemy, the player can perform an enemy-specific attack with the z key and can often do more interesting things than jumping with the jump key, such as limited flying, hovering, teleportation, or inverting gravity (for himself). The game is a bit easy, but fun enough for that not to be a problem and with plenty of secrets.

The real fun comes from the enemies, though. There's no shortage of interesting guys to take control of, including fire breathing elves, giant fireball-spraying robots, pogo-stick guys, jellyfish that climb walls, trident-wielding jetpackers, witches, tanks, suits of armor, and robots that can toss their heads and invert gravity in midair (a personal favorite). Name an attack, its probably in there. The levels vary greatly as well, including autoscrollers (and not just one direction either), caves, outdoor areas, horizontal only levels, flashlight levels grab 6 keys levels, and of course the standard icy platform levels. Theres levels making good use of almost every host body's abilities (or at least parts of levels), and you can go back to previous levels with new enemies to get to new secret areas or just for fun (although you have to make sure it doesn't die, or you're stuck with the enemies at hand).

There's only a few gripes. First, the bosses, up until the actual fight with the other ghost, are way too easy (in the too short vein more than the too pathetic vein, a bit more health would do them good). Some of the enemies are almost entirely useless, and I spent a bit too much time going to previous levels to grab a good host body to start the next one with. Also, many of the enemies don't use the attacks against you that they use when posessed, and while thats a relief with the statues, for everyone else its a shame. The overall difficulty is once again begging to enter this list, although I never really had a problem with it I'm sure a community such as this might.

Still, its great, and if you can play it, DO!

Wow, that sure is longwinded.

#48995 12 2005-02-01T22:02:44Z brickman
Warning: slightly off topic

Am I the only one who thinks that, graphics aside, exile was a bit better than Avernum? Well, sure, avernum had features exile didn't, like people joining the party and more quests, but I think there were more areas in which I preferred exile than Avernum (notice, however, that I have only played exile 3, but have played all 4 Avernums and gone through everything in the free version of all but #3, and the one I spent the most time with of the Avernums was 1 so some of this may not be accurate for the others). Like the magic system--what were they THINKING? I mean, exile's magic system was PERFECT, forcing you to travel and find multitudes of people and perform multitudes of quests if you wanted every one of the numerous and varied (somewhat) spells, but then in Avernum, not only can you get half the spells in the game from the same person (or just by starting with high spell skill), but they only have one spell per level (on average, some have none) and no way to directly buy spell points. The system of spell levels ended up getting warped so badly that if you didn't buy a spell first and you got an improved version as a quest reward or from a spellbook you literally couldn't learn it ("you mean that you can't teach me the level 3 spell I just earned by saving your life because I haven't been taught level 1? Can't you teach me level one first then?"). Plus, the area of effect spells were replaced by "multitarget spells" which completely ruin the balance (especially in the first Avernum), because you don't even have to use any strategy and can zap spellcasters on opposite ends of the battlefield. And what happened to scrying in the third game? It was one of my favorite things in exile 3, but they didn't even bother in any of the avernums. One of the biggest other things they did wrong was making maps and food both unnecessary (seriously, who told them that only needing to eat one unit of food when you do completely unnecessary and useless "rests" made more sense than having the whole party eat every day?) and less desirable to collect. I don't care if holding 500 rations is unrealistic if the alternative is having a week's worth of food take up enough space to reduce your carrying capacity by about 50 gold worth of stuff per trip, and there's NO REASON FOR MAPS TO NOT COUNT AS SPECIAL ITEMS. And while having different shops offer different prices for your things does add a nice element, having shops only accept certain items in exile is even better, because there were only a few places to unload certain loot types and every town offered something different. And of course there's the issue of identification, which is a joke in avernum because you automatically have item lore of 20 without raising a single point of stats that increase it there, while in exile it only went up if you paid for it and thus the sages were very important.

Seriously, if it would let me I would have exile installed on this computer, even though I can just as easily take avernum, simply because they took three steps forward and 17 steps back when they did avernum.

Relnor casually purchased a paper (which, by the way, they did NOT have in midevil times), and began reading it as he headed towards the inn. He stopped cold as soon as he saw the main story.

Relnor had been a knight for a long time--he had actually been knighted during the reign of the the previous emperor (yes, upon checking the rp info thread its an emporer, not a king), Almuhd Dietorffson. His post in Aled had been relatively safe, so even though his rank didn't reflect it he was one of the oldest knights (not saying much considering how much danger is involved in their line of work). And yet he knew that the last time this had happened had been before he was even born. He had been told about it by his parents. There had been a fire like this one, with reports almost identical in almost every regard--the speed, the failed attempts to stop it, the reports of human silouhettes, even the rumors of "fireballs" upon successfully putting out a part. And in that case, they had eventually found a wizard to be the source, one of the few who had survived persecution, apparetly driven mad by his power. It took a group of almost 3 dozen soldiers to apprehend him once he had been found, and only half of them had lived to tell the tale. The wizard had been burned at the stake, of course, but the damage had been done. . . and to anyone who had knowledge of that event it was painfully apparent that it was happenng again. He rushed to the back to the palace to inform the emperor. . .

Now, until Tsuki's post I was going to do something somewhat similar to his. But after that, I'm not even going to try for fear of redundancy. Instead, I'm doing something different: I'm going to explain my stance metaphorically.

Here is the story of a king and his son. Now, the people love their king, and he is the best king in the whole land. Under him progress and prosperity are everywhere. However, one day the prince notices that a change has come over his father's actions, very suddenly. He isn't seen around the castle very much and is both bitter to his servants. The prince assumes its merely a phase, perhaps induced by stress from some new development in the affairs with a neighboring nation. But as days turn to weeks, he does not return to normal, and by the end of the month four personal servants have been excecuted and the populace is being taxed nearly three times as much as before. The king almost never leaves his chamber and will not see any of his relatives, friends or advisors. His own son hasn't been able to see him in two weeks.
By now, the prince is suspicious that the man wearing the crown is not really the king but instead an imposter. So he decides to test his theory by checking to see whether the scar that has been on the king's left arm since he was a boy is still there. By his reasoning, if this is not their king he is recieving undue respect, undue power and undue riches, and not discovering this may ruin the kingdom. Is he being disloyal by doubting his father's lordship, or is he being even more loyal by doing this than if he did nothing because he wants to make sure that the honors due to his father have not been stolen by a usurper?

I don't strongly believe that we COULD NOT have a god, although he would have to not be the top student in god school to have made the universe so big and then only paid attention to a handfull of planets. But there's no reason for us to believe he IS there, and I certaintly wouldn't want to spend my life worshiping a false ruler.

(a+a)/(b-a)+a/(b-a)=(b+a)/(b-a)+a/(b-a)

They had been following alongside the Kendaru River as they went towards the fire, and now the time to act was upon them. As the fire drew closer and closer, they all lept into the river and prepared to dive when the flames drew near. No matter how magical their source may be, the fires could never burn under the water, so they were relatively safe. Finding their armor too heavy, the detached the straps leaving them in just a thin sheet of easily removable soft leather (as opposed to leather that would give you any form of protection this is the stuff you would not wear into a fight ever) specially designed to have no loose flaps which could be caught in any smaller brush fires on the other side caused by the large one. When the fire was a mere 20 feet away, and advancing at a rate faster than a light courier horse at full gallop, they held their breath and dove under the water. They tried their best to move in the direction the fire was coming from, knowing that the depth of the wall of fire was only about 60 feet--not a distance that could be made in one dive, but short enough that a man could stay in the water long enough to get past. When they resurfaced, the flames were all around them, with foliage bruning at the alarming rate that it had been for the entire time this fire had progressed. Smoke filled the air, making it hard to regain their breath from the dive. The heat was immense. They took another colective deep breath and dove back under the water. When hey resurfaced again, 3 of them were missing, having suffocated and sunk beneath the river. But the rest of them found themselves at the tail end of the fire wall, which was moving away from them at the same rate it had approached at. They climbed out onto the shore and rested for a moment, regaining their strength and their breath. Then two of them went back to look for their dropped armor and comrades. The Kendaru was a slow moving river, so their drowned comrades were still there, but two of the men were dead before they even reached them and the third was in no condition to travel, rather less to fight a wizard. They were only able to retrieve three of the partial suits of armor, and these were given to the knights. Their swords, fortunately, had been stuck firmly into the mud of the river beforehand and were all recovered.

They then set off towards where they knew the remains of _____(insert a town, because I'm not exactly sure how far this thing is supposed to have gotten yet). They had a wounded (kind of) soldier and their food and mounts were probably ashes by now, and they hoped they would find something left of use in the ruins, or perhaps even a survivor.

Relnor
~~~~~~
Relnor examined the situation in his mind. None of the cages he could see had humans, so while he hoped they had survived he had to act on his own. His sword had been taken away from him, for obvious reasons, but they had left him with the armor. If only it were a full suit, instead of the partial chainmail vest with no padding underneath. It wouldn't do much against even a human opponent, and with their strength the lizardmen would not even be slowed by it. The lock on his cell was fairly prominent, although the key was obviously not nearby. He did, however, have a standard issue knife hidden under his thin armor, which a careful search would have easily discovered. He reached through the bars in his cell and grabbed a stick, one of the ones that had for some reason not been set aflame. He whittled at it with the knife, creating a sharp point on the end. He wasn't any good at whittling, of course, and it took him a while, but at the end he had something resembling a two-foot-long spear. He then attempted to force the lock with his knife. The lizardmen were of almost no skill in crafting, and the lock easily gave. The opening to the cell was now unlocked, but he held it shut so as not to draw attention until there was a lessening in the number of lizards running around, at which point he could flee. Meanwhile, he looked for anywhere he could hide once he escaped, and thanks to the lack of tree cover easily spotted the armell village he had been captured in. He examined the ruins looking for a spot which he could possibly hide in, and finally chose a location inside what used to be a house but had been reduced to a 6 by 6 foot section of wall with one edge supported a foot off the ground by a stump, and the other on the ground. There were large, loose boards nearby, and it would be easy to cover the opening. The main problem was that they might still be able to smell him, and he had nothing with which to mask his smell. Normally this would be enough to make him completely rework the plan, but with so much smoke hanging in the air he was willing to take his chances. Now all he had to do was wait for the right moment. . .

I remember once I woke up, and for some reason (can't remember why) I thought I was lying on the floor of my dining room, at the end opposite the doors (no, I'm not rich, the dining room is smaller than many of my classrooms in school, its just got the biggest table so we eat there instead of the kitchen). Why the fact that I was really in a bed didn't screw up this assumption, I don't know either. Well, I decided I wanted to go to my room, so I got up and started walking towards where the doors would have been if I was really in there, except of course I was in my bedroom and thus it was really about four feet to a wall wih a closed door that opens inward. I also happened to have the misfortune of having a box on my floor at the time (don't remember what was in it, but it had something in it that was fairly solid) and had apparently just picked up all my clothes off the floor. So I end up stubbing my foot on the box, still not realizing it was my room, and step over it. when I reach my door, for some reason it doesn't strike me as off that the dining room shrunk and I begin trying to hit the lights, so I can find and open the door leading out of the room. Except I'm looking for a light switch in the middle of a wooden door. After a few minutes, I get really frustrated, and am about to give up when I accidentally hit the real light switch (accidentally because it was a foot and a half away from where I was looking) and find myself in my own room. And the funny thing is, all of that really happened.

Now, I can't recall when you said you're releasing n's source code, maybe when 1.4 comes out or maybe not, but that doesn't matter. When you do, its natural that people will grab it and turn it into 20 different versions of n with additional objects, enemies and moves. This is a good thing. But the source, as we all know, is terrible. This is bad. This means making modified versions will be harder, and less will be made with fewer changes and take longer to do them. This is very bad. Although someone will undoubtedly just make a version with clean code, by the time they finish others will be well into their own mods and won't want to start over.

What you should do, in my opinion, is get someone to clean up the code before you release it. I don't want you to do it, because you've (hopefully) got other important projects to work on/a real life. Instead, you should give it to someone on this forum who meets two requirements:
A) is able to make n's code much more efficient and logical
can be trusted to fix the code and give it back without doing anything else with it, especially making his own mods or distributing it

I would suggest for this task a moderator, preferably Tsukatu. We know he has inhuman programming prowess, and I'm pretty sure he's responsible enough to not distribute it until you're done. Once its edited, it will be given back to you, and you can not only distribute it when you're ready but also use it as a much less CPU-intensive base for future updates (if and when they come). When the mod community gets their hands on it, the results will be much better and run better.

Whoa, I just made a huge extreme mode run, from 11 all the way up to 16. And it stuck too, to those saying it won't record passing 15. That was just. . . amazing. And of course, I used the x cannon a total of 0 times.
Its weird how skill in this game works. You first play it, and it seems entirely mindless. But for every level you pass, you begin slowly gaining skill and technique, but the funny thing is, when you get to the end of your 5 level run that looked impossible you have NO IDEA how you did it. I mean, you knew what you were doing, but the strategy springs up when you're using it and then just vanishes. I mean, I just did mine, and yet I can't tell you what I did to weave through the boss shots, just that I did, did well, and can do well next time. I don't think I've ever experienced a game where I couldn't put the strategy into words (some where those words would fill a novel, but always some ammount of words). You just either have it or don't.

BTW, is anyone else surprised by how this thing never lags? N lags even when its the only thing open sometimes, and the most complicated n level can't hold a candle to one boss fight here in terms of excuse for lagging, yet I have never seen TT lag.
