#55908 24 2005-03-25T14:20:38Z brickman
Yeah, I sort of planned my rpg around both MMO and single player things at different times, and in the end they both ended up becoming very different games which just happened to mesh the same genres and happened to share a combat system. The MMO would have had a focus on fighting players, with everybody being divided into two "empires" as well as most of the npcs (including the normally neutral ones like orcs and goblins, which would have tribes on both sides). Instead of normal leveling, you would raise fighting skills by "purchasing" training with a combination of gold and "loyalty" points, which would be gained by killing people/monsters on the opposite side with more points from people and the most from high levels or large battles. Towns would be loyal to either side, but if you launch a big enough organized force to completely push the enemy out of a town you could take it over, realigning all of its shops (of which each town would have different ones) and thus denying members of your enemy's army of certain services (such as a helmet store) while giving you an extra outlet for those things (aka now you can go to two towns for a high-grade helmet). There wouldn't be any restrictions on the PvP conbat/conquest, except that large battles may have to be divided into several smaller, slightly overlapping ones. But if you pushed them back until one army only had a few cities while the other controlled the map, the game would automatically implement the "automatic 2-army preservation" switch and the losing side would be joined by something big (like minotaurs) until they got back a few towns. The idea is to keep them from being completely wiped out. If they ever got reduced just to their capitol, I would give the victorious troops some reward for "winning" the MMO and then go in and reset the towns and realign the people (randomly), and let the game continue from square one politically (but without resetting players).
But, of course, often the act of planning is the best part of game design; I seem to be addicted to thinking up and fleshing out games I konw I have no chance of ever making. That combat system would lag to hell with anything more than three players, I bet.

Edit: oh, forgot to say, everything after "two empires" would be true of the MMO but not the single player, whose plot has nothing to do with this one. Yeah, the only thing they have in common is the combat.

Nonono, the traveling and town stuff is not in that view, it switches to it during combat. Look at how many non-roguelike rpgs use the same screen for combat as everything else.

And of course, one of the big things for any game I make would be cutting the F***ing crap. Summoned creatures shouldn't be useless (actually, I think the single player one would involve a lot of summoned creatures). Shops should not pay you 25% of what they will sell something for (considering that my game would be more focused on the money than stats, I may even bring it up to 90% so that its less a penalty and more a discouragement for getting cheap upgrades). Food should be used up on a daily basis instead of if and when you rest, and how much should depend on how many people you have (you would be amazed how many rpgs fail one or both of these or just skip eating all together). Cardboard cutout enemies should not make up the majority of the game. And for the love of god, combat should not be boring. Yes, fixing the mistakes so common that they're the norm is one of the most important reasons I have for wanting to make games, and probably one of the reasons I am always thinking up ideas even when there is no chance of me making a game.

#61917 18 2005-04-24T23:06:10Z brickman
No depth? I think that if you take a step back, you'll notice that 2d games can have MORE depth (or less if its a piece of crap, but we aren't talking about those right now because they apply to all genres). Take, for example, the typical action of attacking (not defense, not combat in general, just the offensive part). Now, watch as I analyze possible methods of attack from various types of games:

2D
-platformer: just about anything. You can have guns, karate, swords, ninja stars, killer yoyos, grenades, eat monsters, jump on heads and take over their body, or just be forced to evade/flee enemies, to name a few. You can also have any combination of the above with any variations of range/speed/power, with or without ammo and with potential of 360 degree aiming within your 2 dimensions.
-fighting game (aka Street Fighter 1-1 type or Little Fighter free-for-all type): in addition to the multitudes of punches, kicks and sword attacks you can potentially give a single fighter, with jumping or crouching ones included, you get access to huge numbers of combos and specials ranging from fireballs to summoning a sword to lasers. And every single one varies from character to character and varies in speed, range and damage.

3D
-FPS: Basically, hit a button or two to select which gun to fire, and then use your mouse to aim a crosshairs at the enemies. Click, hold down, duck behind something to reload. Pray that nobody is behind you, because you would probably never know since you can only see about a fourth of what you can in a 2D game. Exceptions are grenades, which ricochet and must be aimed higher than you mean for them to go, and the occasional melee attack which involves holding down a "walk/crouch" key while inching towards somebody's back so you can, you guessed it, click on him.
-fighting game: well, I suppose they've got the 2D tied for this category, but there's a lot bigger selection in 2D

rpgs have been omitted because they can pretty much work the same way no matter what the view is

So there we go. A 2D victory and a tie.
"But wait" you say. "Thats not fair, because in FPSs you also must use cover, which means crouching behind a box and running over to anoher box whenever someone throws a grenade. So combats a lot more involved." To which I say: see soldat, 2D has you covered too.

#2667 1 2005-04-26T21:32:58Z brickman
Alright, here's the character thread for out Avernum rp. I would suggest that we avoid non-human characters this time, definitely no non-humans if you're coming from the surface. We need at least some new arrivals as well as established people, and all arrivals should know each other. I've got two similar ideas for my character, either one could work. I personally think the first is more interesting, but I can't quite make up my mind so I'll put both and let you choose one:

Profile #1
Jhonathan lives in Formello with his brother Bernie (an npc from the game), the alchemist. But to say he lives there is a bit misleading. More often than not, he is out on journeys to patches of rare alchemical herbs scattered across the caves which he then brings back to his brother. He knows about dozens of patches that noone else does, and is always on the lookout for more, but many are located a good distance from home. The patterns of their growth and ripening generally determine where he goes. The roads of avernum can be dangerous, of course, especially for lone travelers, but he is usually able to defend himself thanks to his inside track for potions--he can afford to respond to almost any threat with a potion of strength or speed, and if he ever gets in trouble he can just quaf some healing potions. He has in fact undergone a form of training to allow his body to accept these potions more easily; through a little-known process that would drive anyone not directly related to an alchemist broke, and the result is that a few sips of potion for him will yeild the same results as quaffing the whole bottle for most people, although the effects usually wear off sooner. He is currently preparing for a trip which would take him to the area near Fort Avernum, a long journey indeed but to a patch of herbs that many people would kill to know of--the legendary mandrake.

Profile #2
Richard was an alchemist on the surface, making potions for members of the Emporer's army. He specialized in potions made from herbs found underground, which he believed to provide stronger effects than their aboveground counterparts. He was quite wealthy, with a good place in the hierarchy. All this ended when one of his rivals decided to gain the upper hand by replacing some of his herbs with poisonous ones. When one of his healing potions intended to speed the recovery of a wounded captain killed him, the years of loyalty meant nothing. #62808 15 2005-04-29T20:55:41Z brickman
I think the sound/wailer drones could be good if you changed it slightly. Here's my take:
Sound drones are not bound like the other drones, when you are within a certain range (lets say 2 or 3 inches) and either jump, run, land or wallslide, they will hear it and home in on the last spot they heard the sound from. Unless you're jumping or you let go of a wall, this means you're getting it. We'll say they move at up to the speed of missiles, but instead of turning they will just accelerate in your direction (not all at once, and they do have to slow down first if they're going away from you), and bounce off walls. I can picture it in my head but I'm not quite sure I can describe it right in words. The best way to deal with them is to leap over their heads, since they can't track you in the air, and then run at top speed as they hurriedly turn around to chase you. This is pretty nice, but the real fun comes with tracker drones there as well. These basically sit still until they see you and then move like the sights for a gauss turret, but without the restrictions of staying in its line of sight. Instead of stopping and shooting, however, these things will emit a loud noise whenever they're tracking you which overrides normal sound drone behavior and causes them to home in on the trackers. However, the sound drones will pass through the trackers, and if you keep moving they'll always be targeting the area behind you, so you're basically being chased by a crazed homing drone which is bouncing off the walls and nipping at your tail. This is the real cool part, and it may not even be worth the bother to have them function without trackers because the trackers are what makes it good. Maybe they don't do anything until the tracker is activated and you place them in the level paired with the tracker (like with doors).

One of the most interesting dreams I've ever had, although I'm not sure how many times I had it and haven't had it for a long time, was this somewhat realistic one involving our car. I would be sitting in the back seat, presumably waiting for one of my parents to come outside and drive me somewhere, and suddenly the car would leave park and start moving. I would be startled, and after of course yelling at the top of my lungs I would climb up into the front and try to stop it. But this was long before I learned to drive, and I either didn't want to risk hitting the wrong pedal or it didn't work (or maybe I just didn't think of it, dreams often work that way). So as it left the driveway I would start turning the wheel and desperately try to just not hit anything, all the time moving at about 5mph yet still seeming too fast, and I would invariably end up turning it right, towards Livingston (a very busy street, one you don't want a little kid who can't drive with no brakes crossing) and I would end up weaving all across the street like crazy, and I actually don't remember whether I hit something before waking up or just wake up, but I never actually see Livingston and the main thing I remember is just that feeling of panic when it starts and the complete lack of control as it moves. This one realistic dream is worth 50 weird funny ones, if you ask me, because I remember it even though many more interesting ones are forgotten by the time I reach school (and thats just counting those that I remember upon waking).

#2747 1 2005-05-05T22:08:43Z brickman
I just did episode 29. More specifically, I did the first half last night, left it open, and just did -3 and -4, but thats besides the point. Knowing that this was widely viewed as the hardest level up to this point, I decided to use the NTTS for 29-3. You wanna know how much it helped? The only thing I gleaned from it was how best to do the last fall. His guide for this level included the statements of obviousness without strategy ("From the start, walljump up the shaft, avoiding the guided zap drones, then emerge out of the shaft and head left" without telling you how to do it--I could say that if I had never played n before) which are rampant throughout the site and an unnecessarily long route for going down the shaft (people using the guide are looking for beating the level, not the speed records), and acts like his strategy for getting back up is objectively the best. Using the picture makes it a little better (and uses a different route than the text), but still can't help with getting up. 29-4 is even worse, as I'm not even sure the method he used in the pic is possible since every time I tried it I ended up hurling myself against a rain of bullets while jumping down into the middle area, and everything after the first switch in the text is so confusing you're better off figuring it out yourself than deciphering it. I realize I may be overstating things a bit, but I'm not trying to put down Maniac here--just saying he needs to change the guides.

But anyone can berate a guide, right? So instead of just berating him, I'm turning this post into a guide for both those levels. Here goes:
Quote: not really a quote but I'm using the tag anyways
29-3

This is held by most players to be one of the most frustrating levels in the game, and after playing it for a while you will undoubtedly agree.  The difficulty spikes midway through, but don't give up--you'll have to redo the first three.
First, evade the drones by running left and wallclimbing.  While instinct tells us to make three hops and get onto the flat ground to jump out, I have found that if you instead follow this wall for FOUR jumps, using the fourth to cross to the right side so that all it takes is one more tap to get you out, you will succeed 100% of the time (once you know what you're doing), whether the drones chase you or not.  Doing this part efficiently means you can spend more time in the hard part and finish sooner.  Once at the top, descending into the pit is a simple matter of falling down to the uppermost slope and then running right.  Don't take any chances on the thwump, he's not worth it.
Now, here's the hard part.  I can imagine everybody having their own opinion on the most efficient way of getting up, and which is best probably varies from person to person.  I'll just give my way, in case you can't figure out one of your own.  When coming out of the tunnel, jump on the slope and then wait a half a second before jmping off the wall.  When you do, head for the second jumppad from the bottom.  It takes some expirementing to get the missile where you won't hit it coming up, but its very possible.  The pad will shoot you up and then the slope above you will send you to the left.  Get up against the left wall and allow yourself to fall almost but not wuite all the way to the jumppad below you, then make a quick walljump (landing on the slope right next to you) to crash the missiles above you.  Hit the pad, walljump, and get yourself over to the middle area.  It sounds a lot longer than it is, but its still not one of the fastest routes.
Now, for the last area.  It doesn't really matter whether the chaingun drone is up top or on the bottom because its the same technique either way.  Jump so that you will fall between the middle ground and the closest mines to either side (you can do the right if you walljump from the right wall), falling as straight as you can and landing on one of the sloped tiles.  Then wuickly run towards the exit to avoid the potentially most infuriating death in history and fall onto the exit.

Congratulations!  You're almost through this nightmare.

Well, looks like I have some non-computer work to do, so I'll have to do 29-4 later, but in the meantime everyone tell me whether you think this or maniac's guide is better for that level.

#63874 3 2005-05-05T23:48:46Z brickman
Yes, feel free. But would that mean it links to yours from the level list and then to mine from your guide? I suppose yours should come first for continuity, and because its your site, but maybe putting the links next to each other is better (ie 29-3 Bombshelter (remake) how Brickman does it).

edit: here's 29-4
Quote: still not really as quote
29-4

Almost there!  First, start by running right and quickly climbing the wall.  When you reach the top, you're gonna want to grab the switch and then leap across the chasm to the other side, and as long as you leap in time you should be safe from the chaingun's first volley.  Now, here's where I differ from Maniac.  While his technique may not waste any time, I'm yet to get into the center with it without getting shot.  So if you just wanna get the episode over with, wait on the upper-felt ledge until the chaingun on the right starts charging, then drop down to the left just before he does so that he can't hit you.  Don't drop too far, because the manouver is pointless if you can't walljump back out as soon as his spray has passed you, and you'll probably just geth it by his buddy.  But if you timed it right, youwon't have to worry about bullets as you leap across the chasm grabbing the exit switch and the left inner one.  How you handle the remaining two switches is up to you (personally I used the wall to stop my fall, then dropped to the ground and ran around to use the jumppad to get me high enough for both switches), but remember not to trap yourself with lasers above the jumppad and hurry up because things get really messy if the other chaingun comes around before you're done.  You may have to run to the left wall before going into the exit tunnel if he's made it to the bottom of his cycle by the time you're going for the exit, so as to throw off his aim.  Just remember: keep in mind the chaingun AND the lasers before doing anything, and make sure they're pointed away.

#65011 6 2005-05-11T23:24:32Z brickman
Let me explain how the level data works on tilesets:

Every tile on the screen, whether used or empty, is contained in the code. It has a code of several digits for each valid tile type (aka anything you can do with the tileset only), and reads the code for each tile in succession. even if only the first three tiles have something, the code is the same length as if every space had something.
Now, you are both proposing to add more tiles to this. The problem here is, that would require more numbers in the data box, WHETHER LEVELS USED THEM OR NOT. That means that not only would they have to rework the code, but every single existing level would be broken. Every one of thousands upon thousands. Now do you get it?

Its a bit different with items, of course, but we're talking about the tileset.

#2919 1 2005-05-19T20:39:06Z brickman
There's something about the highscores here that really baffles me. You people spend potentially hours perfecting a highscore run, repeating the same level over and over for time, and then go ballistic when it stands for all of 8 hours before being replaced by the guy who had it before you, and complain about how one person literally owns the boards. Yet nobody goes for the scores that are likely to stay yours for a while--the episode scores.
Think about it. Firstly, my opinion is that an episode score holds MORE value than a level one, because being able to do well 5 times in a row in different settings is a better display of skill than doing well once after not doing well the previous 99 times. And even if you don't, there's no denying that a score that requires a full episode of fast runs in one sitting to topple is going to stay yours a lot longer once you get it than any of the level ones. And it gives people who can't normally get on a chance, since the people who dominate the level runs are somewhat out of their element. If nothing else, someone who comes up with a new strategy for a level will find his improved score goes a lot longer if its used in an episode run that requires competitors who are in a hurry to just improve that one level to be bogged down with the other 4.

So why does noone really go for them? I obviously don't expect the episode scores to be maxed out, but there's really noone trying. I chose episode 34 at random, worked out how the level scores add up if you subtract 90 from all but the first, and compared to the episode score. The level sum is about 207 seconds, the actual best episode score is 198.550. Doesn't sound huge, but I know that one any (and I mean ANY) individual level 8.5 seconds of inefficiency won't last a second. Even if you divided it up, 1.9 seconds on any given level is a huge difference. The difference between the 0th and first places on the levels are .025, .400, .225, .300 and 1.250 seconds, while the episode difference is 15.825 seconds. Its worse on newer levels, where even though the lists have filled up I watched a 0th place demo last night where less than half the gold was snatched in gold-rich levels. Why do the episodes get shunned?

#67987 7 2005-05-19T21:33:14Z brickman
Quote: glenno14, May 19 2005, 03:19 PM
mgs 4!? why havent I heard about this yet!

Because E3 is where the people you expect to hear these things from first hear about it first. E3 (which stands for electronic entertainment expo, for those who care) is where all the major companies making or publishing games show off what they're making at the time, often with the first glimpses (or mention) of a game in hopes that their unveiling will attract more attention than the others and always with new demos and screenshots. Its basically an industry-wide publicity competition, where everyone competes to make the most gaming magazine editors say "whoa, I'm devoting a page to that one for sure." They may show off a demo from a partially made game, or a new graphics card, or a new physics demo, or even systems. Anything that'll get them some mention.

Its a wonder that most gaming magazines don't make the issue right after E3 twice as large as normal.

#69480 4 2005-05-25T20:54:04Z brickman
Yeah, it took me a while to be able to do bounceblock jumps consistantly. You really only need to be able to do a single high jump, that double-jump thing is only for highscore freaks and maybe a handful of userlevels made for the aforementioned elites. All you really need to be able to do is exploit the extra momentum from a single jump while the block moves up. Basically, fall on it from a decent height, and make sure that you're always holding left or right as you push it down, which usually means alternating or slowing down from the jump that landed you there (you get nothing if you fall off), and then while the block is moving upwards hit the jump button full force to make a jump high enough to suit any realistic needs you may have.
As for the enemies, there's no cut and dry formula of "do this, this and this and they'll hurtle into a wall every time," that really is practice.

#70059 28 2005-05-27T21:35:12Z brickman
Castle of the winds is too easy if you ask me. Its got some nice features, but it feels like its a "roguelike for the easily frustrated" more than a game for avid gamers. A lot of that is because of the save-anywhere-and-in-as-many-files-and-as-many-times-as-you-want feature which made many things, such as identification, either useless or easily exploitable and made the strategy of anyone with detect objects be "Save. Enter new floor. Cast detect objects. Check maps. If there are fewer than 5 extreemely valuable magic items and three spellbooks, reload and repeat." And it is also in part due to the dungeons which don't redraw upon reentry and the magic system which let you become a powerful mage without compromising your other abilities (physical combat, defense, running) at all because you automatically get new spells every new level regardless of whether you use them or want them and can easily buy spellbooks at general stores to boot. Yeah, that and the lack of any really strong enemies (the fact that you inevitably reach the point of training on elder dragons and greater demons the same way you had one bears and wolves earlier in the game is one of my pet peeves with roguelikes and rpgs in general, but you reach that point really quickly in CotW).
And I think I remember playing skyroads. . . pretty good, but I remember it being pretty hard too. . . and too many special tiles.

I hate people who respond to any stuck person with "watch the highscores". 95% of the time, if you go to the highscores you'll find that instead of showing you the easy way they show the "three times as hard but it shaves 1.725 seconds off your time so the top 10 or so people all did it" way, and if you look at the bottom ones you either get the "you're gonna be hurting for time when you get to the end of the epsidoe" way or the "I was totally clueless and just muscled my way through" way, neither of which are gonna necessarily make things easy.

For 7-0 it is possible to use the jumppad near the start to quickly get to the top, and you kind of need to distract the chaingun for that top button. For 7-1, you want to alternate between the side blocks and the middle ones near the top in order to get enough height. On 7-2, make sure you take the time to get on the side of the circle that your destination is on BEFORE jumping or you'll have trouble, and ignore the clock. On 7-3, I think it may be easier if you get all the buttons and then when getting the exit switch just jump across and go up through the other door. 7-4 is easy if you don't get yourself trapped in the exit switch room and approach the exit from above.

#71162 15 2005-05-31T03:11:28Z brickman
When you break a game you find something the author didn't intend you to be able to do that can basically be used to "cheat" in a sense. Often breaking involves skipping areas of a game entirely with something the author thought was impossible to do (see some 05-2 demos for a good example), or finding a shortcut or "easy route" through a level that wasn't intented to be usable, or finding a "sweet spot" while fighting a boss that makes you not get hurt by many or all of its attacks, and other such things. Breaking a survival map would mean finding some kind of "infinite loop" which allows you to survive indefinitely by doing the same thing over and over (and since survival maps are about seeing how long you can survive, a path that allows infinite survival is the worst thing that can happen to it.

#71379 2 2005-06-01T01:59:18Z brickman
Yes, teleporters an be a bit annoying if you don't know the secret to keeping him alive. But its your lucky day: I'm gonna tell you the secret *FOR FREE*!

Once you place the jumppad, enter frame-by-frame mode and hit the teleporter. On the second frame of n shooting away from the teleporter, put your mouse cursor where n is because thats the exact spot where you need the destination pad. It only works if you come out on exactly the second frame, no more no less. Not quite sure where line is drawn by the game between powerful jumppads that will just be stronger and telepads that will only work on the second frame, but thats how it works.
#71381 3 2005-06-01T02:08:51Z brickman
A moving wall is basically a thwump that moves backwards and ignores EVERYTHING behind it, including tles and the level border. Once activated (and they're activated by touching or almost touching them) they never stop moving (and thus remove themselves, if you can survive that long). 86-3 is the only "official" level with any (and its one of the usermade levels), but many userlevels used the concept too. Their main use is to force the player to either move quickly or be squished, although they have some other uses (like the bottom row of 86-3). Making one that moves right is simple, but other directions are for some reason extreemely hard to do (requiring off the grid placing accurate to a few pixels).

1) mmorpgs, which are stupid and shouldn't count for this discussion because they require you to either play 24/7 or not play, even if its not fun at all. The entire goal of the game is to become the most powerful by throwing the most time into it.
2) fighting games, by which I mean 1 on 1 games like soul caliber. I really don't have or want to have any reason to belittle this genre, in my opinion any good game in this genre should be addictive, although they can sometimes be hard to find amidst the sea of. . .
3) fps deathmatches, which usually either offer something unique or do something better than competitors to make them stand out and be played longer, but the problem is that there's so many of them that there's no reason that you should be "addicted" to any (since there's a;ways three more just as good of the same type).

You notice a pattern, don't you? All of those (except #2 sometimes, though everyone still prefers multiplayer) are addictive on the sole principle of being multiplayer. You aren't addicted to the game, you're addicted to live opponents. If you had to play them against the computer, 90% of the time you would get bored pretty soon.

2d games, however, are usually MADE to be addictive. Every genre is made for the purpose of being addictive--platformers like n, platformers not like n (I think the gap between games like N and Jumper and games like castlevania and megaman is big enough to count as two genres, in my opinion), racing games, scrolling shooters, and. . . oh who am I kidding, you aren't going to read half of this. I dare you to read and respond to this entire post. I dare you.

#72295 19 2005-06-04T18:24:54Z brickman
You know what? I think that the talk about the bounceblock has made me realise (or think I've realized) just WHY this happens: the bounceblocks and walls have mass, while the oneways and doors are only one pixel thick in terms of how the engine regards them (regardless of how they look). When you walljump on a bounceblock or tile it works normally, but something about having just a single-pixel thick line makes it screw up when trying to walljump, so he can only do it if the game counts him as clinging to the wall. But fortunately, you can work it so that he counts as being pressed against the wall without actually grabbing it and losing momentum by just holding onto the arrow key, so it doesn't look like it.

Ah well. I'm pretty sure I've got the first half right, anyways.

#72343 5 2005-06-04T22:01:59Z brickman
I liked HL2. A lot. Only thing I really didn't like was the occasionally slow pacing (although that sort of didn't ruin things too much), how hard of a time I had with getting used to the vehicles (which greatly contributed to problem #1), and the ending.
I think that it could have done with another chapter or two, but I wasn't really left saying "man, only __ chapters, what a ripoff." And any length gripes I could have would have to be quelled by the sheer number of people making mods to extend its life and the free expansion thing they're making (Aftermath). What it could really do with is a BETTER ENDING. I mean, I played HL1, and when I got to the second half of Zen after beating the giant spider/headcrab mother boss, I literally had to use god mode for the rest of the game because it was THAT HARD (and this was on easy mode, I don't even remember if I had the patience to REACH that boss on hard), and while I do think it was too hard I know that every inch of that would have been extreemely rewarding if I had been capable of doing it. And the final boss and ending sequence were cool. In HL2, I did the entire citadel without really breaking a sweat thanks to the insanely powerful upgraded ggun and the chargers which gave you 200% health and full armor every time. I didn't even really enjoy it, since I wasn't being forced to treat the ggun as a ggun as much as an electric gun (all I had to do was charge at them until I was within the arbitrary primary fire range, and one or two blasts killed a group of six). Aside from grabbing energy balls I only used secondary fire once or twice. And the very end. . . even if you're not going to give us the boss we were expecting, give us something more climactic than a pair of gunships (which would actually have been pretty climactic anywhere else in the game, but here it was just "grab energy ball from generator next to you, turn 20 degrees, shoot" repeated about 5 times for the pair).

As for Ravenholm, I'll quote what I said right before Keron told us to split the topic:
Quote
For some reason Ravenholm was not all that scary for me. I mean, I'm sure it was a little scary, but ten times greater than the fear was the feeling that "This is so sweet. . ." as I chopped groups of zombies in half at once with sawblades and smashed them with cars and set them on fire and (despite not being the least bit bloody or extreemely effective I always liked this one) just pummeling them over and over with a paint can until it stops moving. But when I came out of that door and watched those zombies playing up on the roof, I literally said out loud "You gotta be kidding me. Flying sombies?", but in a good way as in "cool". Of course they don't really fly, but it looked enough like it. I suppose the scariest part would be when you're calling the elevator, of course. "I'll just make sure they don't get in this door". . .
So basically Ravenholm was perhaps the most fun part of the game, because every inch was just violent fun with you thinking "now how am I going to mutilate this next group of zombies" every time you enter a new room. I guess it actually was a bit scarier near the end than I let on in that post, mostly in the parts where fast zombies did roof assaults and that map where you go through an entire wing of th city just to be told you're going the wrong way (mainly because of the respawning zombies).
The vehicle parts. . . well, I have to address them seperately. The airboat chapter, once I was used to steering, was supremely awesome (both the boat segments and the indoor ones, actually) until the part where they attach a gun to it. Now this should make things more fun in theory, but I am yet to master the art of moving at high speed with one hand and aiming a machinegun (which is a weapon that intrinsically requires you to keep the crosshairs centered on any strong target without allowing them to stray, which is impossible when you're moving) with the other. I simply couldn't do it. So I ended up creeping through it, always making sure to stop or almost stop the boat before doing any fighting that involves an opposing force stronger than three combine footsoldiers, and just going past any combat I could while just shooting wildly in hopes of knocking out one or two of my dozen adversaries as I pass to save health. It was slow paced and not too fun, but it was generally much more effective than anything else. And it made the scene with two armored cars in an open area and the final fight with the chopper hard and more than a bit annoying. The car section was basically the same as the second part of the boat one but slightly better due to the obvious differences between the gauss gun and he machinegun and because you had to do a lot of footwork too without worrying about ammo at all. And because you could just floor it through a lot more if you wanted.
My favorite sections were the first airboat part, Ravenholm and everything between getting the pheropods and the end of the "Nova Prospect" chapter (basically, the entire part with antlion allies plus the brief segment where you're seperated from them, because its so beautifally orchestrated to make it still feel like they're helping/coming for you). In no particular order.

As for mods, I can't find too many that are finished. I would love for people to post some finished (or at least fully playable without any huge problems, I don't really care if its in its 27th testing stage or not) mods, preferably some single player ones.

#72522 7 2005-06-05T14:40:40Z brickman
Hey, I don't think that the HL1 ending was lacking at ALL. The last few levels were so intense I couldn't even finish them all, leading up to not one but two bosses who are both bigger than you and BOTH could be viewed as important (hey, try to tell me taking down the haedcrab mother is not going to help anyone) and who both make you feel awesome when you beat them. Definitely didn't leave you feeling like you were shortchanged. And the ending cinematic, in my opinion, was actually a pretty good ending, leaving off at the perfect spot--it leaves you with just enough questions. The HL2 one, however, is the oppoasite--no bosses, no crazy difficulty, no coolness, no feeling of accomplishment, and that ending accomplishes pretty much NOTHING. The idea was for it to be the opposite in the sense that the first was an entirely organic area, where you knew you weren't getting any more ammo while the second was an entirely metal environment with infinite ammo, but it ended up being opposites in the wrong ways.

But lets change the subject to something more people LIKED. Like, all the "imaginative" things you did in Ravenholm. One of my favorite things to do was to gfet out the gravity gun when I enter a room with one of the fan traps, and instead of turning them on like normal just give them a jolt whenever someone gets near. Sure, turning it on is a bit easier, but this way was much more fun and could be used to keep that one that flies off from breaking. Another interesting thing I did was that when I got to the part where Gregori sends you a lift, instead of just standing my ground up there against the zombies I jumped down onto the street (taking some damage, but there's medkits on the other side) and then let the zombies pursue me through the streets and the building as I made my way back up. Not only was it cool, it wa also effective--I got up there again at the same time that the lift did, and the zombies can't get through the trapdoor, so you just did the whole challenge without wasting a single bullet of ammo and with only one fall's worth of damage, which the meds on the other side can more than handle. Its also really fun spawning a lot of rebel and zombie npcs to have either a "watch someone else go through ravenholm" situation or just some huge battles. If only spawning important npcs like alyx and gragori worked right. . .

Things like, say, a huge list of shop items and prices, or textbook magic items like "shortsword of fire" and "longsword of lihtning", tend to be necessary (or at least the first is necessary, the second just acceptable) in an rpg but not really of any use in a roleplay. Same for experience levels, though thats thankfully not present, and often even spell lists can be done without in the name of creativity. And stuff like "tamable" dragons and "tamable" titans (both of which seem ludicrous in and of themselves) should not be needed to be stated, since it is assumed that if a situation arised in which taming one would be possiblt our characters would be able to do it whether you said so at the beginning or not. There is a BIG difference between what goes in a game and what goes in a roleplay.
Third, you might want to include more description of the races. I mean, most of them are fine, but there's nothing I dislike more than somebody just going "well, you already know how humans are, so no point making a description for them or making there be anything special or useful about the humans at all. Its not like anyone ever plays as a human anyways". We know how humans are in the real world, but there's no saying we know how humans would be in a world of magic and dozens of races and undead. If anything, you should be not giving a description of elves and dwarves and trolls and orcs and goblins, since I already know what 95% of rpgs make them all do.
Fourth, thats too long for most people to read. Heck, even I got bored halfway through.

To be honest, I kind of skipped past some of the spell lists and shop lists and similar things. But I'm going to scan them now.
Issue #1:
Quote: kai, 2005-06-06T14:56:58Z
Silver:
Used for currency. 50 silver adds up to one gold.
Copper:
Used for currency. 100 copper adds up to one gold, 50 copper adds up to one silver
Well, there's one problem.

Issue #2:
How would the pandorin crystal's possesion stuff work? Can it happen to the player? Can the player even find possesed crystals? Does the player have to fight possesed people? Does someone who's possesed maintain some control or does the crystal completely take them over? Can it be "cured"? How long does it take for the changes to ensue? Also, I think that most of the changes should be internal (although they can have the same effect)--hardenedl bones instead of armor, alterations to the lungs instead of a mask, etc (the strength, speed and regeneration are already fairly internal). Not only would this make them deadlier by allowing them to blend in with normal people, it also seems more realistic then armor extending over the body at will and a bit cooler. Do whatever you want with weapons though.

Issue #3:
Your shop lists seem a bit more in depth than what is normally useful in an rpg. Its nice if you can make things like tent, sleeping bag, ink and paper all useful without draining any of the fun or just requiring them to do anything, but do it last.

Issue #4:
Well, I doubt that even I could make a spell list where I wouldn't have problems with my own first draft, so don't take it personally. I'm just going to do fire for now, you'll probably get the general drift from that. First, fire ball and bolt need a bit more seperation of their damage or else the first would be raher silly. And you probably want to seperate the levels some, because heat wave (which I'm assuming you meant to be cumulative, btw) and pheonix summon shouldn't be level 1. Others seem fine, except the black fireball and lightning ball are identical. Just make sure there's a reason to use every one. If you need something to fall back to in that regard, just make the ratio of damage dealt to mp used vary directly by the damage it deals in one round (with the exception of things like heat wave which would be always more expensive because they could be maintained while casting stuff next turn for extra damage), so that taking someone down with your powerful spells uses up a ton of mp compared to what it costs if you can bring him down with weaker ones (which take longer, thus letting him have more time to kill you if he's one of the toughies--so you have to choose whether someone's worth wasting mp on or not by how strong he is). Maybe even give people of the highest level a free but very weak spell.

Issue #5:
Don't make a required character sheet, that just stifles creativity and shoots yourself in the foot when it comes to replayability and appealing to many people (preset starting items, however, are fine). At the very least, vary them by race. Also, I hope that those backgrounds are a joke. And you may find that not making all the towns identical would make things more interesting.

Ok, here we are. I tried to get a map from the spiderweb site, but the link at the top of the forum page is broken. If anyone makes/has a map, attach it and I'll edit this post to include it. This thing may have already missed its chance, but lets hope it hasn't. . .

Jhonathan
~~~~~~~~
"So, are you sure you've got everything you need for the trip? I really would be devastated if you weren't to make it back in one piece," said Bernie as Jhonathan gathered up the potions he would need and his bag.
"Don't worry, I've made this one before. I've got speed, strength and healing potions in here, and I doubt I'll even need to use any. I mean, they did recently increase the number of guards between here and Fort Avernum," he replied as he added trail rations to the bag.
"Yes, but they're only guarding the paths. We both know you're not going to be following the same route they do, and there are plenty of brigands out there."
"Forget about them," he said, pulling on his heavy cloak and sticking his shortblade in its hidden slot. "I can handle anything I find. Next time you see me, I'll be bringing you two potions worth of mandrake." And with that, he set outto the south, towards Fort Avernum--or more specifically, towards the patch of extremely herbs located near it, his thoughts drifting. It isn't too common, in truth, to have such a valuable patch so close to such an important town without more people knowing about it, but mandrake was so rare that very few people even knew what it looked like in its unused form--it was so rare, the chances of ever seeing one weren't worth the time to train it when you could be learning to find, say, some energetic herbs. Some people regarded it as a myth entirely. He knew that there were few things some people wouldn't do to know the location of this patch, but thats why you have to cover your tracks out here. By now he was already off the beaten path, partly to reduce the chance of someone following him and partly because he knew that nothing useful ever grows near the roads--many times he had found herb patches purely by luck while on his way to a different patch, entirely because he took a slightly different route each time. He would already be passing two lesser herb patches on the trip there which he would sample, and one other was due to bear some fresh herbs at the same time he would pass it on the way back. Oh, what another alchemist wouldn't give to have this boy collecting his herbs. . . but nothing would have been able to convince him to leave his brother and to abandon the city of Formello with no potions. Who needs a group of guards anyways? They'd just make the job harder. . .
Suddenly, the snapping of a branch nearby jolted him into full awareness. He turned quickly, but saw nothing. Curiously, he went over and examined the spot. He couldn't find whatever had made the noise, but he did notice three distinct sets of footprints--only one of which could have been his. "So I am being followed" he thought to himself. "Looks like I'm going to have to pass on those minor herb patches until the return trip, or at least until I can throw them off. . ."

Jhonathan
~~~~~~~~
As he was nearing Fort Avernum, Jhonathan desperately wracked his mind for some way to throw off the people following him. He had already tried stopping in for a meal at the inn in Fort Duvno and exiting the fort from the other side, but they had apparently split up with one person watching each exit and so continued to follow him without actually leaving the underbrush. He decided on a plan. He detoured towards the swamps behind the fort, and once there he stooped down and pretended to be picking some herbs. Of course no real herbs existed this close to the fort, rather less the common varieties that one looks for in a marsh, but common knowledge among alchemists and non-alchemists alike was that swamps were a habitat for numerous useful herbs, so he was sure they would fall for it. As he pretended to examine and pick some random weed located there, he watched the reflection in one of the small pools. Indeed, he saw one of the men beginning to step out, with his weapon sheathed, to get a better view so as to identify what herb he had found and where. He bided his time and. . .
Quickly he quaffed a sip of hasting potion and with unnatural speed he drew his shortblade and plunged it into the man's chest. Only then, seeing the man's armor peieced together from various guards and travelers and the dried blood already on his sword, did he realise his mistake-- these men following him had no idea who he was or what he was doing, they were merely common bandits! And bandits always traveled in packs. . .
Immediately seven more figures rushed from the woods. He managed to wound two more before the effects of his potion wore off, and the others quickly apprehended him. The one who appeared to be the leader sneered at him. "So, you like to play rough, huh? Give me one good reason not to just kill you now?" One of the others opened the pack and began pulling out potions. "Hold on boss, this guy looks to be pretty rich to be travelling with this many potions. Either that or a delivery boy between some pretty powerful people. Either way, he's gonna be worth a decent ransom." The boss thought for a second and nodded. "You're right, this guy could be worth more alive than dead. Consider yourself lucky, boy".

#3308 1 2005-06-15T01:10:44Z brickman
I found an interesting rpg recently called The Spirit Engine, and have been playing it a lot for the past few days. In it, you choose three heros from a cast of nine (with riflemen, priests and mages) and set out on a quest guided (if you can call it guiding) by a mute, defenseless fairy/spirit. There's an intricate, although not necessarily too groundbreaking, plot, and te characters are developed quite a bit (but I think they took shortcuts by making the guys in each row have a set "personality" so that they only had to make different dialogue for each character in about half of the cutscenes). But the main thing here is the combat. It uses real time combat where you have to quickly rotate the order of and determine the next attack of each character, with no fewer than 18 attacks for each character type-but you have to specialize eventually among three or four skills in order to stand a fighting chance, and you have to make sure you have attacks with multiple types for each one or else you'll be buried once you start reaching battles involving monsters which may have three different sets of resistances, immunities and (later on) weaknesses. Its a lot deeper than it looks at first since the various attacks have different speeds and damages and other inherent advantages (for instance, speed shot and chain magic get royally screwed by anyone with a partial resistance but are more effective against those with weaknesses and a certain boss) and each character has two skills to which he has a bonus and two with which he has a penalty (for instance, my priest is the best at partyheal and bless spells but is penalized with the hand of god and holy bolt spells). But it lets you play around and learn the system without fear of screwing yourself for later because there's a guy halfway through who lets you reassign your skill points. And. . . you know what? Talking about it doesn't really give you an idea of how well the thing plays. If you're looking for a new game, try it, and if you're not having fun by the end of the second world (the system stays pretty basic on world one, with only the last boss on the entire first island having a resistance) then go look for something else. But I think you will enjoy it.

Oh, and if you want a hint for your starting party, the three I picked seem to be good: peter (the fighter on the first row), zephyr (the priest on row 2) and eisford (the mage on the last row). The strengths of the first two are exactly where I would have expected and wanted strengths to be for that class (although if you think of fighters as meatsheilds you may think differently) and the same goes for one (but sadly not both) of the mage's. You won't be disappointed (until you get to the point where you're stuck, and you go to the forums to search for the boss you're on and everybody assumes that your priest has 10 levels of hand of the gods which is pathetically slow for zephyr and you never leveled up because you assumed you didn't want to invest points in a skill that was one of his weaknesses)

Hmm, I wonder if there'll ever be a time when I can manage to post a game without two full paragraphs of description. I need to learn to be shorter winded, don't I?

#77667 13 2005-06-23T14:02:18Z brickman
This system may work for the top-end maps, but it groups anything that isn't top quality into one big "0" group. Because very few people would put average or pretty good maps in their list (only excellent ones), so anyone who is currently getting a 3.9 average or lower would probably not get any and thus look the same ratings-wise as the maps that are 1s, 2s and 0s. Plus, just imagine how easy it would be to cheat this system--you don't even need multiple accounts, just a browser with tabs. And all maps ratings would decrease with time and with every time that someone with it as a favorite actually plays it. The first step if you even want this to be a moderately logical system is making the number of views only count each ip once (or accounts). And make a check box for people who like to search but won't be adding any maps to their list to not mess up the scores of any map they view.

Firstly, @TDL: those were Dungeons and Dragons stats, and if you don't know what that is you must officially give up your geeking license and leave the forums. THACO affects your likeliness to hit, and AC is armor class, and both are better the lower the value is and terrible when high. 20 THACO is what a level 0 player gets, and 10 AC is what someone with terrible dexterity and no armor gets (thus, someone having 20 would mean you can't point a sword in his general direction without him running into it pretty much). Blue tetris and Pariah also used D&D rules. And now:

no reply

Time for a reality check:
A) this entire game, and all future games from metanet, was made by just TWO PEOPLE. That does NOT translate to infinite pools of time to waste on every little request
B) you assume that they know enough C++ to completely remake n. I'm not saying they do and I'm not saying they don't, but assuming someone who has only produced anything in one language knows another well enough to do the same thing is a big logic leap
C) translating something to another language is not as easy as pressing the magic button and then going out to lunch while your computer automatically alters the code to fit the new language.
D) doing ANYTHING with n's code is even harder than it would be with most games since it has the sloppy coding that goes along with being a first project.
E) they already have one or more very important projects, and are working their collective butts off already.
F) quite frankly, this isn't even very important.
G) umm, I'm sure there was a G when I started, but I forgot along the way.

Anyways, this was a stupid suggestion that pointed to a user who has no intention of paying attention to the current situation aka a pair of people making games part time and their very first and sloppily coded game.

#3912 1 2005-08-03T22:24:57Z brickman
Just found this nice new game yesterday, and its good enough that I'm sharing it with the community here. Its basically a space shooter where enemies teleport in and you have to kill them. Sounds generic, right? Well, the things that set this apart are the nice way they set up your two attacks so that you really do have a choice of how to handle any situation (not like most where there's a primary attack and a "press this when you're overwhelmed and you'll clear the screen but it has to recharge for 30 seconds" joke of two attack modes), and the great AI. Seriously, this AI is good. It probably uses the cover better than I do, and when its done hiding behind it they rush at you and then stop to shoot at just within the radius of the death explosion while constantly moving to thwart your efforts to kill them. Really, just seeing how well he did AI is probably worth a download.
The only real gripe I have is that the "boss" ships (which take numerous hits to kill but could be mistaken for a regular enemy until they open up with their space machinegun) are completely random (I've gotten one as early as "level" 2 and other times I've reached 3000 before seeing any, and occasionally two pop up at once).

BTW, my highscore is 33800, but I'm sure I'll topple it soon.

1: has at least 4 people already playing it when I join (although I won't quit if people are leaving and I'll bend this if selection is poor)
2: doesn't have a password, survival or advance mode
3: has a ping of less than 1200 (no, seriously, there was one at 1200 when I went on last. I usually ignore the ping in all honesty, but that wouldn't let you in if you tried)
4: is playing either inf, ctf or htf, preferably whichever I'm in the mood for but I won't complain if I can get any of them
5: if at all possible while meeting those rules, has no weapon mods.

If there's several that meet all requirements about equally, I'll take the one with the most people--you're not playing for the time between firefights.

#89119 52 2005-08-07T22:29:04Z brickman
Yay, someone cares. Ok, here goes:

Drill Man
In this game, you play as a little robot with drills for hands (looking like a megaman character, not some crazy chrome tank). Instead of the focus being to make tunnels, however, this game plays in the same vein as games like n and jumper, and the main application for your drills is to cling to and "walk" on walls and ceilings. While on a wall he can move up and down, let go or jump off, and while on a ceiling he can just move to the sides or drop down. There are of course enemies, some of whom can be killed by drilling them from a specific direction and some who can't be killed at all. Terrain includes walls, hard walls (that you can't cling to), breakable blocks (comeon, he's got a drill--why not), spikes&mines, thin platform (which you can stand on or hang from and switch between those positions at will) and similar things. It would be divided into episodes which may or may not require you to finish in one go, and every 5/10 episodes would be a "boss" episode where you spend the first four "levels" fleeing from a ninja (both as a throwback to n and because he makes a good boss) and then fight him on the fifth, with a very specific attack pattern involving running from side to side with his sword, leaping over you throwing shurikens, then jumping between the walls hurling more shurikens between jumps, then jumping to a position above you and doing a "power thrust" straight down, immediately after which you land a blow. Every time you see him he moves faster and throws more shurikens. (Yes, the boss is VERY fleshed out). The rest of the levels would involve avoiding and occasionally (though not usually) skewering the enemies while traversing walls, floors and ceilings to the exit, with gold in there as a bonus. Controll is still pretty simple, wiht buttons for jumping, running, one drill button and the up and down (only for aiming the drill).

How does that sound?

#90080 6 2005-08-12T01:23:50Z brickman
I have never really been religious, although it seems my parents wanted me to be considering they're STILL forcing me to go to Sunday School. I mean, I'm gonna be a Junior in highschool this year, if I don't believe yet no ammount of reading stupid passages is going to make me. But anyways, my logic for not beleiving is this: if there was a perfect and all-powerful god out there, we would know it for fact by now. Not on faith, not from the pages of a thousand year old book, we would know it and see evidence of it as much as the fact that there is air. I mean, there would be no refuting it. In order for god to be leaving us to our own actions this much when we're doing this badly, he's got to be either non-existant or in no way an incarnation of all that is good, in which case he's obviously not the same god you're praying to and thus its not doing you much good. I've already stated the "too many conflicting religions" thing in previous threads, so I'll skip it.

As for the "everything nothing" arguement, there's two holes. First, you don't lose nothing if you turn out wrong, because if there's nothing after life than you're going to want back the large percentage of it that you spent praying and confessing and whatever once you realize its wasted. Second, the assumption that I "lose everything" assumes that my non-belief makes me let myself become a lying, cheating, stealing and generally mass-sinning jerk, which is almost as big of a logic leap as the ones you had to make to have faith. I'm still going to be a good person, I'm going to abide by the laws of society and the rules of morals and ethics, I'm going to give to charity--no intelligent diety is sending me to hell just because I didn't spend some time praying to someone who had given us no real reason to believe he existed. Alright, I've come to a conclusion with the missile challenge: there's no way you can do that without ridiculous ammount of saving and loading over and over any time you run low, because of two things: A) Its impossible to get more without using some, meaning that if you get to one or two you're going to have to have a ton of luck to get more and if you run out (even if you ran out by knocking out three enemies none of whom dropped missiles) its practically game over, and B) The missile dropping is both random and not weighted very high, so if you save with one or two you may have to go outside, blast a group of enemies (thats if you're lucky--you may not have groups always) and exit to the menu 10 times before even getting one missile back. Tibia I've played and come to the conclusion that it sucks. Perhaps not as much as runescape, perhaps more, but I learn from mistakes and after the time I wasted on runescape it didn't take me long to spot the crappiness and ditch Tibia. Any game where they stick a dragon's lair within 5 minutes walking distance from one of the starting towns and don't leave ANY real warnings that would allow you to differentiate it from an orc lair or a normal cave until you actually see the dragon and are being breath attacked for 50% of your health per second, then lose practically ALL your expensive items when it takes you out after a second or two of running, and you had NO WAY OF KNOWING and no warning until you were already dead, is messed up in my book. But even if I ignored that incident, the game seems to thrive on pointless grinding, farming and training on the same baddies, while of course competing with others to just get them, and then for some reason they decided that you should be able to trap players to steal their loot, and every class seems to get the short end of the stick so that you're choosing which has the least disadvantages instead of which has the best advantages, where high level monsters can be lured miles out of their lairs and only players who are high level can outrun them (What the hell is with that? I'm weak so I should also be incapable of escaping the fights I have no way to and was never meant to survive while the people who can handle it have the option to flee? Everyone should run at the same speed), and trading can only be done one item at a time and kill/item stealers are frequent, and orc warrior is to orc as orc is to rabbit instead of just being a slightly stronger version, etc etc etc. It only survives because its popular, but I can't imagine why its popular. At least runescape kept monsters in their respective areas and didn't let you accidentally stumble on dragons, and had a reasonable trading system.

The maple story thing, from a quick look at screenshots, looks like the kind of great idea that is almost impossible to not screw up. It may be good, and I may try it sometime, but I'm not expecting too much.
#92837 4 2005-08-21T01:30:54Z brickman
Just pick a gun and learn it. I suggest not picking to learn the m79 or barret because relying on them pretty much dooms you to remain a noob forever (occasional use is ok, but not if its the only gun you can use), and I suggest not picking the ruger because its the hardest to use. You should either go for the dual desert eagles, the shotgun, or one of the first three autos, because they're good guns and not too hard to learn. The bottom half of the list is all either difficult or of limited use. Also get used to occasional use of grenades, even if just for hitting someone trying to jetpack up a hole next to you from the previous floor. Movement isn't a problem once you understand the fact that you will always run faster the more often you jump while running, no matter what the terrain. Once you've got those basics down (using low intelligence bots may help), just jump into one of the flag modes--dm, pm, rm and tm are all based directly on killing and not being killed and thus aren't as good for new players as ctf, inf and maybe htf (that last was added recently, long after my period being new to the game, so I can't vouch for its noob friendliness), people aren't completely focused on killing because there's something else entirely constituting the victory goals and thus you're more likely to do ok, or at least not screw your team up and end up in last place.
#92838 4 2005-08-21T01:45:43Z brickman
I'll admit I'm jaded against MMORPGs, I've tried several and for a short time even tricked myself into thinking I liked runsecape for a while but have come to the conclusion that they do not mix well with freeware, and what seems to be the norm with them is to me the opposite of logical. Thats why the only one I've ever bought was guild wars, on the grounds that it basically changed almost everything and thus did away with just about every standard problem annoyance and stupidity of the genre while only adding a few of its own (the main one being that its sometimes time consuming to find a party while the npc henchmen are not only less intelligent than any other real players but actually lower levels than any real people you'll find in the area). But anyways, several facets of the genre irk me, including the pervasive focus of your time almost exclusively of accumulating loot and xp by repeatedly killing the same monsters and not really using the multiplayer side intelligently (partying is loose or non-existent while random spawncampers or idiotic moodbreakers are all over). Tibia is no more an exception than runescape (and there's probably at least a dozen members here who will create a rant against runescape on command). And as for being careful I think there's a difference between being cautious and not venturing more than 20 feet away from the direct line between town and the nearest lowlevel dungeon full of a handful of things you will spend the next two levels rekilling. As I said, there was no indication of any kind that there was a dragon. No bonepiles or corpses outside (by corpses I mean scenery ones, not the bodies of players who already fell for it), no giant footprints, no sign, no message warning you that you're 6 levels lower than the game recommends you being in this area, nothing. The closest to a warning was a couple of small fires outside the entrance, but those were identical to campfires I had seen while battling orcs so they don't suffice. And that wasn't the only time I died, just the most illogical. Trust me, by the time a level 8 or 9 or possibly 10 (I don't remember what it was exactly) sees a dragon, he's too close to be able to flee in time.
#92846 6 2005-08-21T03:14:55Z brickman
Um, that assumes of course that you find some nice people who would show you the places, that they're not busy, and that you don't end up with someone who really just wants to get you killed for your loot. And no matter how many nice people there are, there is simply no excuse for having a dragon lair in the middle of a fairly early area without at least something to hint that there's something tough in there.
Oh, and did I mention that I'm generally opposed to the idea of dragons in an multiplayer rpg? Because you see, there's not a single monster in one of these games which doesn't become the bread and butter of a player's leveling grind when they get to a high enough level, and there's something severely wrong with the very idea of someone "training" on a dragon. If you make the dragon be so strong that its impossible for a max level character to kill it by himself, then by all means stick in the holy grail of enemies, but otherwise don't devalue your game and reduce the immersion by having the players train on legendary creatures. And I'm yet to see that un-soloable dragon. When I was browsing the (at the time) new members only feedback forum on runescape after the big update, I remember seeing someone complain that they now needed TWO ITEMS AND A PRAYER to train on dragons without fear of death, instead apparently of the one or two before the update. Yes, it is very good, and an rpg, but the main reason some people don't like it is that it doesn't really start getting interesting untill the second chapter, and the first one is a bit on the long side. During the first one combat strategy is mostly limited to rotating your party so that the damage isn't all to one person, but once you get to world two things get significantly more interesting and by world three its actually pretty complex. Oh, and if you decide to play it don't worry about your skill choices at first--you get to reassign all points at the start of world three, and as long as you don't pick three with the same damage type you can beat the first two worlds with almost any skill combination. Don't even open the help file until you're choosing your real skills in world three.

#94808 17 2005-08-28T03:05:49Z brickman
Alright, after playing Maple Story, I have officially decided that nothing can be worth the time it takes to get to level 10 in order to get an actual class, with actual abilities who can actually DO something interesting/that makes the game interesting. I can deal with a half hour or even a full hour of "training" before the real game starts just because its hard to find ones where it isn't there, but this is ridiculous. However, it took me until I had reached level ten to realize it wasn't worth it, so I could continue anyways. But when I think about it, the lack of attention to fun factor displayed there is very ominous and so I think I'll leave.
With that, I'm going to make the top ten list of things NOT to do in an rpg:
1) Make the player have to level up to get a class. I don't care if you do a locked in class system or picking and choosing skills. I don't care if there's a ten minute training area to get you used to the controls, especially a skippable one. But when you require the player to reach level x before leaving the starting island and choosing a skill (ironically both games in this thread do this), and x is more than 2, you're basically weeding out any players who actually care about playing a game. Which leaves the powergamers and idiots.
2) Concentrate more on the character appearance than the characters. I'm sorry, but I'm not playing an MMO to design a cool looking mage or play dressup. Quite frankly, if I had to choose between having a dozen different choices for every body part plus choice of colors on all items vs only one 16 bit character sprite per class and having a 10% increase in the number of abilities and SKILL variation within each class, I'll take the second any day.
3) Making us do the same thing repeatedly. Now, I know that a bit of repitition is inherent in the genre. But it doesn't hav to be as much as it usually is. Give us three or four areas to explore at any given level instead of one or two, and don't make us kill the same enemy more than 50 times in the same place. And I don't want to associate the word "grind" with your game.
4) Ignoring the advantages of multiplayer. Also known by me as "lite" multiplayer, this basically means neither requiring nor strongly encouraging cooperation. Every time someone accuses someone else of stealing a kill or item, your game loses points. Players should tag team out of necessity, not yell at anyone who tries to fight the same monster they are because the area's baddies spawn slow or they need to get to the area on the other side of it faster or they simply can't handle them on their own. Party systems that give a minor bonus for kills by party members doesn't cut it. You need to make it so the player NEEDS to and WANTS to have a party, even if they're training. A way to help with this is to make sure that no single character can master every skill, or even every skill allowed by his class, so that he needs someone to fill in his weaknesses.
5) Generally speaking, forget that the focus of a game is to have fun.

I think if all or even a good handful of MMOs followed these rules the genre would be so much better. As it is, I can think of one.

He has small weak points in his first form with a lot of health and tons of projectiles, not to mention squishing you, and in form two he summons missiles that, while not as numerous or fast as the previous form's attacks, are annoying in their ability to fly through anything (including the floor, I think) and the difficulty of killing them (not good for healing). The only solace is that you can get lined up to do a lot of damage with missiles, knife, or machine gun from under him and his projectiles don't deal too much damage--but in challenges you almost always either aggravate those small weak points (on a specific weapon one) or those projectiles suddenly become so strong that you simply can't afford to stand under him and suddenly he takes forever to kill in addition to filling the screen. And the fact that it takes so long to get there from the save doesn't help.

Thus, after a certain point the game stops incrementing its difficulty in any form for the rest of the infinite tower. Quote: Lunatic, 2005-09-07T13:18:56Z
So, um, I suppose I should probably present that theory of mine regarding Ballos so as to start the debate...
Consider it done.
Quote
Quote
Quote
Quote
Quote
Here's my theory regarding how the island falling can't kill Ballos, but the island falling can:

Seeing as Ballos' orb form has invincible armor, when the island falls he just changes into the orb, shuts his eyes and weathers the impact. Then he just transforms back into human, and blasts his way out into the surface.

Hey, it's simple, and it works, right?

That would work, except the orb seems to only be used when he's in danger. If you didn't notice, he WANTS to be killed, but for some reason can't allow himself to die. Thats the only reason he's defending himself at all when he's just asked you to kill him, and definitely the only explanation for him putting up such a good fight to the full extent of his powers (otherwise he would just do the first form for show and let you smash him). The ballos ball only exists to defend him if his foe proves too powerful.

I'd say being inside an island that's hurtling down towards the earth would be considered "in danger"

That reminds me of a question regarding games: when bosses have multiple forms, and notice you've managed to defeat their first form, why don't they just change right to their final form and obliterate the living guts out of you? It'd skip the bother of going through the intermediate forms

I think the answer depends on the boss. Some enjoy toying with you and want to see how far you get (overconfidence), some expend a lot of energy or are otherwise hurt by changing form (example is the doctor's second form, or one where the boss ends up just getting more aggressive/desperate near the end). Some may just not want to risk any knowledge of their true power getting out. Some might realize that if they skip to the final form and you beat it they've got nothing left. And some may just do it for cinematic effect (aka all of them).
Come to think of it, most bosses tend to not have more than two distinct forms, even if their attack patterns change numerous times. Its mostly just final bosses of really boss-focused games.

Ah, you got me on that one. But I'm still ahead in the Ballos debate.

Quote: Raigan, Sep 10 2005, 07:13 PM
Quote: glenno14, Sep 10 2005, 10:23 PM
A 5 year old can play N? I better get my little sister to start playing N then 
actually, we got an email from someone who had three generations of their family playing! i think the youngest was their 7-year-old daughter.

i think my favorite email of all time is this one:
"
And so today, as I saw the exit screen and read the message "this game is dedicated to the brave ninjas everywhere...", it occured to me that the game could be viewed as a very interesting social satire.

In fact, one of the basic premises that we impose upon ourselves as we begin playing is that the robots are evil - when, actually, they are so faceless and mechanized that it hardly makes sense to judge them at all, or at least any more than we would an elevator.

Further, our hero's motivation is unclear, and yet we assume him to be a hero although the only thing he seems to do is steal. Everyone loves a non-violent crook, so is he 'the good guy' because he is fighting against the odds or simply because he is the only thing in the whole game world that seems to posess a soul?

This brings me to the sorroundings - the aspect of the game I find possibly the most meaningful. Each uniformly grey level can indeed be seen as an allegory - either of bureaucracy itself or a dehumanized, bureaucratic society as a whole. Each level is intricately unique on countless levels and yet it all boils down to the same thing: getting enough gold to survive and moving on.

It takes some passion, skilled dodging and serious effort, but by the time you realize it, the grey machinery has already consumed you - you are, after all, a gold-craving puppet in a world populated by soulless robots that is much too large for you to understand.
"

Thats great. That was pretty funny.

And I still find it hard to picture a five year old playing n. My little sisters (who are just now five) watch me playing all sorts of videogames all the time and even have favorites and their own names for them (n is the "shadow guy", cave story is the "robot game" only after I told them that he was a robot and thats why he doesn't have a mouth), yet when they recently tried to play the first level of the easiest game on my hard drive (one I kept around mostly because they loved to see it), both of them were incapable of even moving effectively--they couldn't jump over a bump in the road without a lot of work because they wouldn't hold down the right arrow key while jumping because they couldn't figure it out. They didn't even scroll the screen far enough to see anything capable of hurting the player (enemy or pit) before giving up. I'd say that 0-0 requires more coordination than the first two levels of that game combined.

First, it would have to recalculate that value every time you beat a level if its figured offline, and calculating it online is impossible since it would need every player's score on every level and the list would take forever. Second, it leaves no feasible way to verify it if somebody cheats to get a ridiculously high score. Third, some levels would make more of a difference than others (a guy who competed for the highest score on a complex level with tons of gold and multiple paths would have an advantage over someone who fought long and hard for two consecutive scores on really simple/tiny levels like 59-0 or 59-1), and if you're the type who competes on some and ignores others they don't like (which I think most do) it'll take days to get the levels you didn't want to devote time to before to be competitive enough for this.
