#101786 240 2005-09-18T18:50:49Z brickman
Tips:
1) You're not going for highscores. Take your time. The timer in n s evil not because it actually is likely to kill in most episodes but because even when there's plenty of time it puts you in the habit of rushing. You should have more than enough time.
2) Try to develop ne specific path, including the timing of that path. The drones are confusing since every one has a different algo so your odds of figuring anything at all out as you go is low. Watch them for several seconds after you die to see what the drone(s) that caused the death were and were about to do so you can figure a way to avoid that particular death next time (even if thats just to get you five seconds further to the next stopping point)
3) You don't actually have to go on the right side of the screen at all. If you didn't bring a lot of gold with you from the earlier levels you may need to, but its possible to stay entirely on the left half of the level. What does this accomplish? Well, the right side is slightly more dangerous since there's more mines and if the configuration of drones when you do reach the button is like mine it may not be feasible to go right at all from the button opening that side. You really don't need that gold unless you're really slow or a highscorer. I had taken my time on the previous levels and not gone for all the gold on any of them, yet I finished with 20 some seconds left--a lot more than it sounds like since you don't have another level behind it.

#104709 8 2005-10-01T00:23:36Z brickman
On the topic of the matrix and the spoon:
I was so bored one time that I actually analyzed the spoon thing and how Neo was able to freeze bullets, and after a while I actually figured out a logical explanation. The program makes you be whatever your perception of you is/what you "know" you are (Morpheus said this and then demonstrated it in the training sessions). The way to manipulate all the stuff is simply to convince yourself that the spoon is part of you that you can control, or that you can jump between buildings, or whatever. Once you do that, the program adjusts itself to the fact that you can do that, and now bending the spoon or leaping 50 foot gaps is as simple as opening a door. "There is no spoon. You have to realize that when you bend the spoon you are really bending yourself." Its a bit harder with bullets, since you have to convince the program that they're a part of you during the time between firing and hitting, but if you can't handle it I suppose there's always the slightly less awe-inspiring alternative of just making your skin bulletproof.
Pretty deep for something that most people will never bother to think about and just dismiss as nice-sounding stuff made up randomly for the sake of letting the protagonist be learning to understand something.

#4788 1 2005-10-16T17:13:12Z brickman
Have you ever seen a franchise or style of gameplay that was cloned and copied so often you had trouble figuring out why people had liked it in the first place? Thats me with megaman. I mean, sure I like platformers, and shooting is obviously the most sensible method of offense when making a platformer, but I couldn't get into a game type where the whole levels were literally filler and all of the difficulty and skill was consolidated into instant-death platforming and crazy-tough bosses, while you'd be hard pressed to build a level with the existing components that a good player COULDN'T easily beat without either of the above despite the number of enemies. Not to mention that getting stronger with each level means the levels you put off become easier.
But then I came across Hardhat Rebellion 3, and I get it. Everything fits here. The above problems melt away and are replaced by great gameplay, attractive graphics and music, good level design, and good boss weapons. I can't really explain why its good, but anyone who likes or doesn't like megaman type games should play this. And to top it off, once you beat the first 8 levels it gives you a "weapon" that lets you skip the worst platforming bits or even all of them if you pour all the ammo into it.

Damaged Games
I can't speak for the other two games because all three are convinced that I have a gamepad, which I don't, and only the third lets you "skip" configuring it.

Quote: Ngaged, 2005-10-30T14:12:20Z
I'm not interested in the Urban Dead stuff, either. Eating brains sounds extremely boring...
Urban dead is a game sort of attached to the brain-eating site. Basically its a low-tech MMO where you play either zombies or humans in a quarantined city of undead. Both sides are composed entirely of players, and the humans have a wide variety of paths they can go down for experience (healing, axe or gun training, running DNA scans on zombies and reviving the ones who look like they're slain human players) or utility (barricades, searching improvement, free-running, and so on), while the zombies are limited to just combat but still have a variety of skills for improving themselves in various ways (faster movement, stand up faster after being shot, increased claw and bite effectiveness, etc). The game sort of favors humans in many ways, but there are a few advantages for the zombies (like being able to select targets and not having to search for ammo), and more importantly the zombies have recently become very well organized near the center of the map and are putting up a huge fight, with a cluster of suburbs ranging from dangerous to suicidal for humans (sadly, the rest of the map is almost all human territory). The only thing that might annoy some (aside from being primarily text-based instead of graphics-based--although its not obnoxiously text-based like those really old games and it has buttons and a visual map) is that you're only allowed 50 actions each day (and for low level zombies movement and standing up count as multiple actions), and that forces you to budget your moves and doesn't let you play all day (although you can have several characters and there's a very active forum), but this really increases the strategy and is part of the core of the game (not just something tagged on at the end to save his server or get little kids to bed on time). The community is very strong and I've recently been spending more time on their forum than this one, and it actually makes the game twice as much fun.
I think you should all try it, and those that tried it a year ago and couldn't find anyone else on should try it again.

It doesn't increase immersion because for the most part they only deal with things you wouldn't normally want to do in real life, for example I don't go around breaking windows to see how it shatters or building forts out of desks and blowing them up yet thats the sort of stuff the physics engines allow you to do. More important, they add almost nothing 90% of the time. I fully support giving realistic physics to things such as gravity or momentum for players and enemies, because that enhances gameplay. But being able to roll barrels down the stairs for fun doesn't add anything. Unless you're directly enhancing gameplay with it, such as the grav gun in half life 2 (and I think even with that they did far more physics than they really should have, I traded framerate and cover thats invisible from a distance for some extra ammo for their marketing department), your physics are junk, and unless they're implemented very well physics objects in sidescrollers do nothing that normal level design couldn't do. Finally, they are a ridiculous strain on both processors (which n already kills thanks to being their first excercise in coding and being in flash) and developers.
Show me a mockup screenshot of a level where your physics objects would create a fun experience that can't be accomplished (or almost accomplished), and I may retract my disproval. Maybe.
#115524 9 2005-11-16T22:38:01Z brickman
Bodies not sticking out of walls is not physics. Being able to destroy debris in your path does not require physics (though everyone seems to assume it does). Jumping up and then falling back down with some damage if you fell too far isn't physics. Grenades aren't even really physics, at least not in the sense I mean. Look at duke nukem 3D. In there you could toss pipebombs, take damage for jumping off buildings (and damage that depends on the surface you land on no less), use jetpacks to enter through windows or fly around between roofs, go swimming, ride elevators and subways, drop people on conveyor belts and have their body get carried along, blow up walls or in one case level an entire building, and so on--all without a physics engine any more complicated than "If object is not resting on ground, make object fall". You could even set up explosive tripwires, bounce shots off walls, and shrink and then step on your enemies or yourself, and set up decoys to distract enemies in a firefight. All without physics. Really, the lack of physics didn't create any barriers at all to what the program could do--what few real barriers there were were caused by the rigid sector system instead. However, it ran fast and well, was fun enough that there's people who still think fondly of the features noone bothered to copy from it, could set up fairly realistic and interactive environments if you wanted it to, and never, ever had enemies standing behind solid walls that you couldn't see because the game needed to take shortcuts just to keep up with its massive drain on resources. No, I'd like to see more games rejecting physics, not trying to "improve" them.
And BTW, N already is affected by physics more realistic than you'll find in many platformers. He has real momentum which can change directions as a result of terrain, has gravity that kicks in gradually instead of all-at-once, can move fast enough to smash himself against any surface but needs a boost to get above a certain speed threshold, and handles sloping and even curved surfaces in a very believable way. Physics affecting n do translate into better gameplay. However, his enemies have no physics effects at all, because that does not create better gameplay.

#115593 11 2005-11-17T04:29:34Z brickman
Yes, I think I said that physics which translate into gameplay are good. If it can be used by you in a fight or to avoid a fight, or better yet if you can get AI to use it, physics are good. But most physics systems don't care about that. They care about being able to pick up a bottle and carry it across the room, or shoot out a window and watch the glass fall, or push a car into the water. If physics systems are letting you bank boulders off cliffs into enemy cities, go physics. If they're letting you barricade your room against the zombies (provided the game also gives you zombies who are both strong and smart enough that you really need that barricade, which with the abundance of machineguns most games fail to do), power to them. If its letting you toss a paint can through a window (I seem to be fixated on windows here for some reason), go invest in your AI scripts instead.

#116145 13 2005-11-19T14:35:49Z brickman
I think physics engines inherently hurt the game? Why? Because if their marketing department is going on about physics, then they're not going on about AI or gameplay, which means they're not WORKING on AI or gameplay, at least not fully. Time spent letting the player toss books through broken windows is time not spent letting the player shoot up an ambush of soldiers or lob rockets at tanks. Resources spent on physics are not going towards AI or towards graphics or towards *gasp* making the game actually run at a decent framerate and letting you see all objects from across the room (seriously, in HL2 there must have been a dozen spots where I could see someone hiding behind a table or a bookshelf or in a few sections a piece of the wall (apparently one which gets blown out later, but at the time its a solid concrete wall) and I tried to shoot at them just to hit their invisible cover, and several where they couldn't see me but I could see them because a very large physics object was between us). Immersion is nice, but its nice as an exception, its nice to occasionally play an immersive game after a half dozen full action games. But these days EVERYONE want to have that immersion game, and if every game is "immersive" it doesn't mean anything anymore. I really didn't feel immersion in HL2 at all. I was impressed with a little of what it was doing at the beginning, and I may have jumped when the zombies in Ravenholm crashed through the skyroof after I thought the door was secure, but no immersion. You can't have real immersion with any restrictions on what a player can do that don't exist, and you can't have those in a game. I can't just drag a heavy object in front of a door in a game like in real life, if its too heavy to lift above your head you have to get all the way behind it to push. I can pick up a TV and pull out its plug by moving it too far from its socket, but I can't actually go to the plug and pull it out like a normal person and I can't put it back in, and if I can change the channel there's no more than five choices and probably less. If I knock over a barrel in real life its pretty easy to right it as long as its not too heavy to move, if I knock one over in HL2 its almost impossible to set it back up without finding another barrel to rest one end on so it can "fall" into a standing position, and even then its very hard. These intricacies can never all be done, and if they could more would arrive in their stead. Games will never feel like real life, so why should every game in development try?

#116172 15 2005-11-19T15:23:07Z brickman
I'm not saying that realism or graphics don't enhance things. I'm saying that any physics that don't directly affect gameplay are worthless. If a game has enough action to be a good action game you won't have a chance to mess with most of those physics anyways, because even if there were times when you're not fighting you'd want to be heading to the next fight because its more fun than toying with trying to see how close they came to real life.

You'll notice I repeated an awful lot of examples here. Thats because those are good baselines to use. Barricades are one of the easiest to talk about examples of physics applied very well, and shooting out windows or throwing random objects is the best example of useless physics. And dissappearing walls and crappy framerate on even the lowest settings are the best examples of their cost.

It is, but you don't get it until chapter 5, and since 5 is almost entirely a story chapter you don't get to use it until chapter 6 (I think there's a total of 15 chapters but am too lazy to check). To make up for that, though, chapter one is also mostly story and pretty short, chapter two is half story and easy anyways, and you spend the majority of chapter four piloting a sweet airboat/motorboat that makes for some very fun action sequences, so its really not that bad of a wait to get it and they make very good use of the gravity gun for the rest of the game. As long as I'm mentioning the special chapters, chapter 7 and the beginning of 8 are spent in a buggy equipped with a laser (although I didn't find it nearly as cool as I should have), the very end of seven and the majority of eight you get to controll an infinite army of expendable flying antlions intent on killing your enemies, and in the second to last chapter your guns get stripped and the gravity gun is upgraded so that you can actually pick up living enemies and chuck them at their allies, or can grab orbs of energy from generators and use them to disintegrate attackers. Yup, you should be drooling by now. . .
edit: not to mention, of course, chapter six, aka Ravenholm, where you trek through a survival horror-esque destroyed city filled with zombies getting scared and blowing the crap out of them, and in the second half you start seeing fast zombies who move at your speed and can jump between rooftops and climb gutters, and black zombies who throw poisonous headcrabs at you that temporarily shut down suit defenses making you instantly vulnerable to one-hit kills. #118288 36 2005-11-26T21:36:41Z brickman
I don't think its a big deal at all. Woot, it makes slightly more realistic graphics, it has the RAM for slightly more physics, and you're going to pay a mint for it. The games are not going to change, you're still going to be playing the same stuff as you did on every other system in the last few years with a facelift. Truely good games, the genre-rocking games that get cults behind them and are still remembered 10 years later, have never, ever been caused by hardware improvements. Its the software that counts, and the software is going to be the same at best and may very well follow the worriesome trend of putting even more of their staff on "box art" (aka graphics, physics and anything they can stick a large number onto) and fewer on making the games fun. Stick with PCs, where there's always going to be someone concentrating on gameplay no matter how much the giants put into graphics, and where YOU choose when its time to update instead of letting them tell the entire gaming world that its now time to update and if you don't RIGHT NOW you won't be able to get anything, even if it doesn't really require the resources of the new system, and all your games aren't going to work on your new rig but they'll sell you the sequel with more of the same gameplay for another 50 or 60 dollars (not to mention that when everyone upgrades at the same time to the same thing they've got a bottleneck for extreme gouging, while PCs regularly cycle and if you try to get whatever the newest PC today is a month from now you'll pay half of what they'll still be charging for the Xbox 360).
To those who point out that you need updated equipment to play PC games, I'll point out that you don't. You can play new games on hardware a year and a half old and probably use the highest settings, and I'm not sure how many PCs there are still out there that couldn't do at least something with Half Life two, even if it doesn't look pretty or run fast without upgrades. Wheras new games coming out now will not work on Xboxes that were top of the line until only weeks ago. And in response to the "console exclusives" or "long wait for Halo" arguements, it works both ways--Half Life two has been out for quite a while and is just getting ported to the consoles, sans multiplayer too.
And as a side note, other than the two other people I think my computer (which is not high end by any standards) has seen stuff as good as that first pic on half life two (and you know that's the only one that actually represents gameplay), and the gun looks worse than anything in HL2 to boot. And while the car does look true to life, I see no reason our computers couldn't handle the other two--at least in cutscenes, which is what they are.

Better tip for the muscle doctor: your only defense is the distance between him and you. Not only is this the only fight in the game in which if you run under him when he jumps he'll pound you, his charge attack and jumping attack can only be avoided by backing up. His teleport, which isn't nearly prolific as in the other fight, isn't too bad. And yeah, you need him down fast. Usually I unload as many missiles as it takes on him immediately and end the fight before he has a chance to do anything--misery's summons will get you some of those back before you'd need them in the final fight, and if you've got spur you don't need them for the core at all. It may give machine gunners a few less missiles against the core, but if you let him buttslam you or summon the bats its really not worth the ammo you're saving.
